#8942. Want to Ride More at Home? These 9 Stationary Bikes Make Training Easy, Quiet, and More Consistent

Find the right at-home ride, whether you want a budget spin bike or a premium smart-bike setup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Weather and daylight don’t always cooperate with our riding schedules. And when we add work hours, family time, yardwork, and life’s daily grind, finding time to ride can feel impossible. Especially during the dark days of late autumn and winter, indoor riding becomes the only realistic option for many of us.

Luckily, indoor cycling is no longer the boring, arduous task it was only a decade ago. Today’s stationary bikes range from no-frills machines to fully connected setups. Some even feature live and on-demand classes, immersive virtual rides, and easy syncing with popular fitness platforms like Strava.

All of our editors and test team ride or train indoors for at least part of the year, sometimes even during the summer months to escape the heat. We’ve logged countless hours on stationary bikes and standard indoor trainers. In our testing, we’ve wrestled with finicky machines, endured glitchy interfaces and endless updates, and spent plenty of time grinding out virtual miles from our basements, garages, and home gyms; some of our editors have even taught spin classes.

Stationary bikes come in three main styles: Upright, recumbent, and dual-action. Upright models feel most like riding a traditional outdoor bike. Recumbent bikes offer a more reclined position, while dual-action bikes add upper-body work to the pedaling action.

Our testing and reviews focus on upright stationary bikes made by cycling-specific brands and general fitness companies. To differentiate between the two, we call models from fitness companies “exercise bikes” and those from cycling brands “indoor bikes” in this story.

Exercise bikes by fitness-oriented brands often feature a more upright riding position, multi-position handlebars with foam padding, and wide, comfort-style seats. The pedals usually have toe clips for use with running shoes.

Indoor bikes from traditional cycling brands typically mimic the body position, ride feel, and functional layout of outdoor bikes and feature dropbars, brake hoods, adjustable crank length, and narrow saddles. They usually feature high resistance for sprint workouts and virtual racing. These bikes used to be expensive, but prices have dropped over the last three years, making them a great choice for everyday indoor riders (not only hardcore enthusiasts).

The BowFlex C6 has the most capability at a reasonable price. High-quality and adjustable, this bike features Bluetooth connectivity so you can connect to apps like Peloton, Zwift, and Schwinn Trainer to join community rides and track progress.

The monitor displays time ridden, speed, mileage, heart rate, and resistance level. It doesn’t show wattage or precise RPM (it displays them on a scale). However, it does measure them, and you can see that data if you connect it to third-party training apps.

The flywheel is smooth and heavy, and you can crank the resistance up significantly through 100 incremental levels via a knob. Toe cages let you ride the C6 in regular running shoes or flip the pedals over and clip in with Shimano SPD cleats.

A great feature is the unit’s silence—you can use it day or night without waking your family. It comes with a forearm heart rate monitor and a pair of 3-pound dumbbells for light upper-body workouts while riding.

Want a more immersive experience? Check out BowFlex’s Velocore. It features a 22-inch integrated console with tons of class and entertainment streaming options, and is compatible with Zwift, Peloton, and JRNY.

If you don’t like traditional exercise bikes and want something that closely replicates the fit and feel of riding your actual bike, the Zwift Ride is an ideal solution—and the recently updated V2 model addresses issues our editors experienced with the first-gen model by adding adjustable crank length and saddle setback.

At its core, the Ride is an indoor cycling setup that eliminates the hassle of constantly mounting and unmounting your bike from a trainer or dedicating one bike solely for indoor use. The frame is exceptionally sturdy and has proven itself time and again under the stress of multiple test riders’ workouts. Paired with the reliable Kickr Core 2 trainer—our Best Overall smart trainer pick—the setup delivers a premium ride experience.

However, the real magic lies in its seamless integration with Zwift’s virtual world. You can join races, group rides, guided workouts, or explore immersive digital landscapes alongside fellow “Zwifters.” The most popular virtual cycling platform globally, Zwift succeeds by stripping away the monotony of indoor training. It gamifies the experience while offering social and competitive features that you can engage with as much—or as little—as you like.

The Schwinn IC4 is ideal if you want quick, easy access to ride metrics; you can see your data on the display—no subscription necessary. It also has a stand for your phone or tablet, USB charging for your devices, water bottle holders, and weights so everything you need is at your fingertips.

If you’re in the mood to be pumped up by a live class, Rouvy, or Zwift race, the Bluetooth option lets you jump right into third-party apps. The bike comes with a free two-month subscription to Schwinn’s platform, JRNY, which offers workout programming tailored to your preferences and over 200 virtual courses.

If you like the concept of the Zwift Ride but want an indoor bike with more adjustability and refinement, Wahoo’s Kickr Bike Shift is one of the best options. It’s essentially a stripped-down version of Wahoo’s super-premium, $4,000 Kickr Bike Pro; the Shift doesn’t include the Pro’s motor-electromagnetic resistance, gradient simulation, and some finishing details. While nifty features, they’re overkill for almost every indoor rider.

Like the Kickr Bike Pro, the Shift is quiet, super smooth, and easily adjustable to fit multiple users in a household. It also features standard bicycle component attachment. This makes it easy to replicate your outdoor bike’s fit on the Kickr Shift with your favorite saddle and handlebar. If you want the convenience and silence of an indoor bike, and a premium indoor riding setup, the Shift is the one to get.

Peloton redefined at-home fitness with its original bike—a sturdy, low-maintenance machine built to withstand years of sweaty daily rides. Its true draw, though, has always been Peloton’s vast library of on-demand and live classes, now spanning not only cycling but also running, core, and boot camp sessions. With the Peloton app, you can even take workouts on the go.

For years, the bike itself saw few changes—until the Bike+ arrived. It keeps the durable frame and quiet belt drive but adds a redesigned handlebar and a larger 23.8-inch touchscreen that rotates 360 degrees, making it easy to follow floor-based workouts. The model also features forward-facing Sonos-tuned speakers and auto-resistance that adjusts automatically to match instructor cues. Not everyone will use it, but those who do will love the convenience.

The most notable update is Peloton IQ: a built-in camera that tracks your movements, offers real-time feedback, and counts reps. There’s even a small fan above the screen for added comfort.

However, these upgrades come at a premium: the Bike+ is significantly more than the standard Peloton Bike. If you want to save $1,000, the standard Bike features solid build quality and full access to Peloton’s unmatched training ecosystem. But it doesn’t include auto-resistance, high-quality speakers, a rotating screen, Peloton IQ, a phone tray, and a fan.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike features a 35-pound flywheel and provides a smooth, quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable with a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches. Riders can also adjust the handlebar height and the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Although the Yosuda doesn’t connect to third-party sites, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned on the included single-button monitor. Below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame provides stability and durability, yet it’s easy to move thanks to the small wheels on the front edge.

If you’re spinning on a budget but want a connected experience, the Echelon EX-15 may be the stationary bike for you. This high-quality bike offers access to proprietary classes you can stream with an Echelon membership ($399.99 billed annually). Echelon’s membership isn’t limited to cycling content. The subscription offers rowing, running, strength training, yoga, and more. Enjoy workouts to music from artists including Pitbull and Lady Gaga—plus dance, EDM, hip hop, K-Pop, metal, Latin, and R&B.

The EX-15 bike itself is sized perfectly for smaller spaces, yet doesn’t skimp on comforts like an extra-large cushioned seat and padded handlebars. The mechanical knob lets you adjust resistance between 32 levels. You also get a free 30-day membership when you buy the EX-15 through Amazon.

It’s important to have one with solid construction and high weight capacity if you plan to put your stationary bike through the wringer. The Sunny Evolution Pro can withstand your most intense intervals and feels stable doing it. The 135-pound steel frame has a large footprint with leveling stabilizers in each corner to help prevent rocking.

Complementing that is a hefty 44-pound flywheel, which eliminates the inconsistent resistance you can feel near the top end of lighter wheels. The adjustable handlebar moves up and down and front to back, so you can dial in a position that's comfortable for your back, neck, and wrists.

The seat height accommodates riders with inseam lengths from 29 to 39 inches—a downside if you’re on the shorter side (Our 5-foot-2 barely made the cut, but awesome if you’re taller).

The Evolution Pro’s simplicity also makes it a great pick. Without Bluetooth connectivity (or even a monitor to display metrics), you can exercise without getting bogged down in numbers and be more in touch with your body at different PRE (perceived rate of exertion) levels.

The Keiser M3i is a studio-level spin bike with a clean, streamlined design and simplified interface. It has everything you need to nail your numbers in a hard workout, and then upload that data to apps like TrainingPeaks or Strava. The smooth flywheel is quiet, and its rear location means fewer sweat droplets land on it, so you can worry less about corrosion or wiping it down perfectly. The small monitor displays your power, cadence, time, gear, heart rate (if you’re wearing a connected strap), and total distance.

The media tray holds a phone or tablet above your handlebar so you can follow a route or guided workout as you ride, and it automatically uploads each effort in the included Keiser app to track your progress.

The saddle height adjustment uses preset stops; however, the wedge system lets you place the saddle in the precise spot you prefer. The looped handlebar is comfortable for a wide range of reaches, and the height adjustment accommodates riders as short as 4-foot-10 and as tall as 7 feet.

Stationary bikes come in three main options: upright, recumbent, and dual-action. The bikes recommended here are upright style, which puts you in a position that mimics how you’d sit on a traditional bicycle.

Recumbent exercise bikes seat you in a slightly reclined position with the pedals out in front of your hips rather than directly below, which can be easier on your back and neck. Dual-action exercise bikes have handlebars that move in and out, so riders incorporate their arms into the workout as they pedal.

Look for models with adjustable saddle height and position, plus adjustable handlebars. More adjustability makes it easier to find a comfortable riding position and get a good workout. Like a regular bicycle, a proper fit is crucial for the best experience. I like my indoor bike’s fit to match the position I ride outdoors.

All bikes feature bar-height adjustments, and some models let you adjust reach. Saddle height and setback adjustment options are also a must-have. They also have graduated markings, making it easier to get back to your preferred position after someone else uses the bike.

A dropbar offers hand positions that mimic road bikes, while a traditional bullhorn bar will be more familiar to those of you who frequent studio classes.

The two most common methods for regulating an indoor bike’s resistance are friction and magnets. Friction-based systems use leather or synthetic pads that press against a flywheel—It’s a simple, effective way to add precise, linear resistance. These resistance systems don’t require outside power to operate.

Magnetic resistance is quieter than friction systems. They use magnets (adjacent to the flywheel) to create an electric current that resists the wheel’s rotation. By increasing the current (strengthening the magnetic force), you have greater resistance. With no contact between the flywheel and magnets, this type of bike may offer a smoother ride than a friction-based one.

Some models use electromagnetic resistance controlled by software from a connected app. This allows platforms like Zwift to replicate hills and wind.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Bluetooth-equipped exercise bikes let you transmit your ride data directly to third-party training apps like Peloton or Zwift for in-ride metrics. If it has ANT+ capability, you can connect to extra sensors—like a cadence tracker or heart rate monitor—and display that data on your monitor or tablet. It’s not totally necessary for an interactive experience.

If you want to join virtual classes but aren’t sure which you’ll like (or you enjoy several), look for a bike with connectivity and media compatibility that lets you join the most platforms.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Most indoor bikes function similarly; the accessories that set them apart. The most basic models are as simple as it gets, just an ergometer with a weighted flywheel and a pad to set resistance. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes like the Peloton, with elaborate software for recorded and live classes.

Decide how much technology you actually need for your indoor rides. Some cyclists want a feature-rich experience with training plans, classes, and group rides, while others want a stripped-down bike that covers the bare essentials.

Measure your available space before buying. If you will need to move it, also check the model’s weight and whether it has wheels.

Seat comfort matters; if possible, test-ride the seat that comes with your stationary bike before buying to make sure it's comfortable for you. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.

Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8941. The 2026 New York City Marathon Was the Largest Marathon in History

More than 61,000 runners—from ages 18 to 90—crossed the finish line on Sunday.

One of the world's biggest marathons keeps getting bigger. On Sunday, November 1, the 2026 New York City Marathon officially cemented its place in the history books as the largest marathon of all time, surpassing the 2026 London Marathon, which had 59,830 finishers.

According to results released Monday by New York Road Runners (NYRR), 61,146 runners crossed the iconic finish line in Central Park (61,529 started the event). That total blasts past last year’s NYC tally of 59,226 finishers—which followed 2024’s record-breaking field of 55,646—marking the third consecutive year the five-borough race has raised the bar worldwide for mass participation.

This year’s record served as a nice topper for a historic run as it coincided with the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course. When organizers first took the race out of Central Park and onto the streets of Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Manhattan in 1976, the event was a bold urban experiment. Five decades later, it is an epicenter of the global running community, with waves of marathoners streaming from the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from 8 a.m. until well after dark.

While tens of thousands of age-groupers, charity runners, and first-timers chased personal glory, the pro fields delivered plenty of fireworks at the front of the pack:

There were plenty of other milestones as well.

#8940. Garmin’s New Screen-Free Fitness Band Takes Aim at WHOOP and Oura With No Subscription Required

The CIRQA band tracks a broad sweep of daily health and fitness metrics, giving Garmin users a fuller view of life on and off the bike.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Most fitness trackers come with a second price tag: a monthly fee for seeing the data they collect. Garmin’s $200 CIRQA Smart Band needs no subscription for core health, sleep, and activity tracking. That sets it apart from WHOOP’s and Oura’s paid membership models. Garmin’s pitch is straightforward: buy the band, wear it around the clock, and check the data in Garmin Connect without another recurring bill. It’s a refreshing proposition in a world lousy with subscriptions.

Very basically, the CIRQA is a screen-free fabric band designed for all-day wear on the wrist or upper arm; the concept is similar to the Whoop band. It tracks heart rate, sleep, HRV, stress, skin temperature, Pulse Ox, and Garmin’s Body Battery estimate. Garmin claims up to 10 days of battery life. The band supports more than 80 activity types, uses your phone for GPS, and can broadcast heart rate to a cycling computer. Garmin pitches the lack of a screen as a feature for riders who want the data but don’t want to wear a smartwatch.

The single button handles one favorite activity, which you set in Garmin Connect. Press it once to start recording and again to stop; the band vibrates and flashes an LED to confirm. You can start other activities in the app, and CIRQA can automatically detect some sessions from movement and exertion data. That keeps the band clean and simple, with setup and seeing the details handled through the phone.

I’ve tracked rides with cycling computers since the days of the fabled Garmin Edge 500. Over the years, I’ve sent those files through Strava, TrainingPeaks, and a rotating cast of other platforms. Plenty of them can tell me what I did on the bike. Garmin’s appeal, and maybe its best selling point, is the Garmin Connect app.

With a Garmin cycling computer, your ride data already lives in Garmin Connect. Add the CIRQA, or another Garmin wearable, and the app puts that training alongside sleep, stress, HRV, and other health metrics. The CIRQA’s unique appeal isn’t any one metric the band collects. It’s that those metrics feed into the same ecosystem as your ride data, giving you a more complete picture of your training in the full context of your day.

That can be useful if you’re trying to make better training decisions yourself, or if you work with a coach who wants more context than your power files and weekly mileage can provide. A hard workout looks different after a great night’s sleep than it does after a week of poor sleep and high stress. Putting that data in one place makes it easier to see when a planned session fits or when it's time to adjust the plan.

Wearable device options are more plentiful than ever, and the CIRQA won’t be the right pick for everyone. Its clearest audience is the rider who already uses Garmin Connect and wants health and recovery data alongside cycling workouts. If your bike computer already uploads rides there, the CIRQA adds context about what happens between them. That connection is the main reason to choose it.

It should also appeal to people who want to track sleep, stress, and activity without taking on another subscription. You don’t need a paid membership for CIRQA’s core tracking, which makes it a good option for riders who want to monitor their daily data without another recurring bill.

The other clear fit is someone who wants less screen time on their wrist. The CIRQA has no display or smartwatch notifications. Maybe you wear an analog watch and want to keep it that way; maybe you’re tired of your smartwatch and want a wearable that quietly collects data for you to check later. If you want live metrics and notifications or even the time at a glance, the CIRQA probably isn’t for you.

Sleep tracking and HRV status worked seamlessly for me. I don’t find much value in comparing one wearable’s numbers directly with another’s. It’s more important for the numbers to be consistent and CIRQA’s were. Its readings tracked with how I felt from one day to the next, and also mirrored the trend lines of numbers from other smartwatches I’ve been testing, which made them useful as context rather than scores I had to chase.

Having sleep, HRV, and stress inside Garmin Connect alongside my ride data made those numbers actionable for me. I’m self-coached, so I’m deciding every day whether to do the workout on my calendar, go easier, or take a day off. Garmin Connect’s ability to bring my on-bike training and the rest of my day together in one place felt like the most useful thing about the CIRQA band.

The band has a single button, an underrated feature, and maybe a Band-Aid, too. I liked being able to start and stop an activity manually instead of hoping the band’s auto-detection caught it, especially for commutes, hikes, and runs. In general, auto-detection did a good job with walks, runs, hikes, gym workouts, and swims. My twice-a-day e-bike daycare trip was a different story: CIRQA picked it up about half the time. If it were more consistent on those rides, the button would matter less. But even if automatic activity tracking worked perfectly, having a manual stop/start button feels useful.

As someone trying to avoid another subscription, I see CIRQA as Garmin’s best alternative to WHOOP. There’s meaningful overlap in the day-to-day metrics, like sleep and HRV. WHOOP packages those metrics more neatly into an easy-to-read Strain/Recovery dashboard. CIRQA’s advantage is the Garmin Connect app, which combines ride data with all the metrics CIRQA tracks, which makes it an easy sell for existing Garmin users. But its lack of a subscription makes it easy to recommend to everyone else looking for a wearable device.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8939. A 24-Year-Old Runner Died After a Medical Emergency in the Final Miles of the NYC Marathon

Rachel Apa was running her first marathon to raise money for Parkinson's research in memory of her grandfather.

Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.

Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.

According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.

Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.

Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.

Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.

"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."

Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.

An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.

Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:

"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."

Before the marathon, Apa explained her decision to run on her fundraising page, sharing how much her grandfather influenced her love of sports and why supporting the Parkinson's Foundation mattered to her.

"He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement," she wrote.

Apa explained that watching him lose his mobility after his Parkinson's diagnosis had made her want to help others facing the disease. She wanted to use her first marathon to help others affected by it, raising money and awareness in the process “for research, better care, and a cure.”

As of 5 p.m. ET Tuesday, the page had exceeded her $4,000 goal, and reflected more than $28,000 in donations.

#8938. I Wish Yoga Studios Would Stop Trying to Sell Me on Their Teacher Training Programs

Los Angeles-based yoga instructor Ramoni Overton questions whether a common trend across yoga studios is negatively affecting students. Overton is the creator of the YouTube channel Yoga With Ramoni.

I was brand new to yoga when I first experienced a teacher training sales pitch at the end of class. I had stood up after Savasana feeling pure bliss, practically floating off my mat. But suddenly the instructor was pedaling the studio’s upcoming yoga teacher training (YTT) to the entire room. I was surprised, but I mostly brushed it off, assuming it was a one-time thing.

But then it happened a second time. Then a third. And a fifth. After I heard the exact same sales pitch multiple times, my post-class high vanished before I even made it to the front door. It was replaced by a single thought. “Seriously? Again?”

This experience isn’t unique to me—it’s been happening to many other yoga students. And, in my opinion, it’s a reason why some of them might quietly not return to class.

As a yoga teacher for four years and a yoga student for nine, I’ve noticed that most students aren’t coming to yoga to build a second career. They already have full days and packed schedules. They’re coming to yoga to unwind, decompress, and experience a single hour in which the outside world completely disappears.

At the same time, I understand the reasons behind the post-class YTT pitch. Yoga studios have bills to pay, and YTT is one of the more reliable revenue streams in a business that runs on thin margins. But when studios push their instructors to pitch constantly (and when some instructors receive commission for every sign-up), the pressure is on. The yoga teacher who was supposed to hold space for you is now knowingly or unknowingly working a sales quota. That changes the energy of a studio, whether anyone admits it or not.

And it adds up to something that’s bigger than one annoying moment. Seemingly everywhere else in life, we are constantly being sold something. Ads interrupt us while we’re watching TV, listening to podcasts or the radio, and scrolling through social media. Yoga was supposed to be one of the few places that wasn’t also a marketing funnel.

Studios don’t need to stop sharing information about their YTT offerings. But they do need to stop treating every student on the mat as a sales lead. There are so many ways to share training info without disrupting the post-class quiet. A simple flyer at the front desk, an announcement on the studio schedule, or a free information session for those who are genuinely curious. Let people come, flow, and leave in peace.

If the training is enticing, students will ask about it on their own. You won’t have to sell them on it.

#8937. The 67-Year-Old Who Raced Two Full Ironmans a Week Apart

Mary Mitchell won her age group in Kona and eight days later raced Ironman California, where she also won her age group. Here's how she did it. (Photo: Mary Mitchell, FinisherPix)

Fresh off a sixth-place finish at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, American professional triathlete Sam Long recently took to Instagram to ask his followers a question. Should he race Ironman Florida on November 7, or give himself another two weeks to recover and race Ironman Cozumel on November 22?

Long wants to secure his qualification for the 2027 Ironman World Championship early, but the question of how quickly to return to racing after Kona is a serious one. Among the responses to his post were plenty of suggestions that he take the extra recovery time and race Cozumel instead.

After all, Kona is no ordinary Ironman. Its combination of heat, humidity, unpredictable winds and exposed terrain takes a major physical toll, even on athletes who have spent their careers preparing for those conditions. Racing another Ironman just four weeks later is ambitious enough. What about racing one eight days later?

For 67-year-old Australian age-grouper Mary Mitchell, that was precisely the challenge.

On October 10, Mitchell won the women’s 65-69 age group at the Ironman World Championship in Kona, finishing in 13:11:46. Eight days later, she lined up at Ironman California in Sacramento, where she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, more than 90 minutes faster than her Kona performance.

And she won her age group again. Even more remarkably, her husband, Andrew, 66, who had also raced in Kona, joined her in Sacramento and won his age group too.

What began as a somewhat improbable endurance experiment ended with three age-group victories between them.

The idea wasn’t actually Mary’s. Earlier this year, Mary and Andrew traveled to Morocco to spend time altitude training in the Atlas Mountains with a friend. During the trip, their friend floated an intriguing challenge. What would happen if a bunch of athletes in their 60s attempted two full-distance Ironmans a week apart?

“He persuaded us that it would be a good human experiment to do, to see whether, at our age, you could do two Ironmans in eight days, and what would that be like?” Mitchell explains.

The plan was for all three to qualify for Kona, race the World Championship, and then travel to Sacramento for Ironman California the following weekend.

There was just one problem. Their friend subsequently suffered a knee injury and withdrew from the experiment. But Mary and Andrew had already committed. Their flights and accommodation were booked and the race entries paid for.

“We thought, well, we might as well go,” Mitchell recalls. “How bad can it be?”

They also had the encouragement – or perhaps bad influence – of American friends Jill and Dougin Walker, serial Ironman competitors who have completed around 100 Ironmans apiece.

“We’ve fallen in with a bad crowd,” she jokes.

For Mitchell, who has completed around 30 Ironmans since her first in 2004, racing twice in eight days was uncharted territory. The closest she had previously come was roughly a month between Kona and Ironman Malaysia.

But Mitchell also had another reason to make the most of Kona.

Mitchell had previously won her age group at the Ironman World Championship in 2019. Since then, however, her attempts to return to the top of the podium had been repeatedly derailed.

In 2022, she was hit by a car while riding on the Queen Ka’ahumanu Highway just 10 days prior, preventing her from starting the race.

In 2024, at the women’s World Championship in Nice, she developed food poisoning the night before the race and abandoned roughly 140 kilometers into the bike.

Then in 2025, she returned to Kona, only to discover that what she initially believed to be a cold was COVID. She struggled throughout the race and eventually withdrew on the run.

“I had three years of thwarted attempts to do the World Championship,” she says.

Heading into 2026, Mitchell and her husband had decided this would be their final Kona appearance. They wanted to experience other races and destinations rather than continue returning to the Big Island.

And for much of the race day, Mitchell’s final Kona appearance looked unlikely to deliver another world title.

Mitchell had hoped to swim around 90 minutes, but the ocean conditions and what she admits was insufficient swim preparation conspired against her. She eventually emerged from Kailua Bay in 1:57:06.

“I had an appalling swim,” she says. “I hadn’t done enough long swimming, didn’t have enough endurance, just because swimming’s not my favorite thing.”

By the time she reached transition, Mitchell had effectively written off her chances of winning: “When I stood up out of the water, I thought, a competitive race is off the table now.”

Rather than chase positions, she decided to enjoy what she believed would be her last Ironman World Championship. Her mantra became simple: “Look after yourself and just keep chipping away at it.”

Despite the heat, wind, and particularly oppressive humidity, Mitchell began making steady progress through the field. She completed the bike in 6:38:10 and started the marathon feeling surprisingly good. She settled into a sustainable pace, making sure to take in adequate fluids and calories at every aid station.

With her husband, Andrew, also competing, there was nobody on the sidelines feeding her information about her position. It wasn’t until she reached the top of the Energy Lab, with roughly 12 kilometers remaining, that an acquaintance delivered some unexpected news.

“She said, ‘You’re first and running faster than anyone else in your age group.’ And I’m like, ‘What? No, come on.’”

Mitchell completed the marathon in 4:23:23, the fastest run in her age group, to secure her second age-group world title.

Ordinarily, the next few days would have been devoted to celebrating, recovering and enjoying the satisfaction of a long-awaited victory. Instead, she had another Ironman looming.

Following the Kona awards dinner and a celebratory glass of wine, Mary and Andrew flew to Sacramento, arriving on Monday with less than a week remaining before their next race.

There was no elaborate recovery protocol, no special preparation, and definitely no attempt to squeeze in additional fitness.

“We rode our bikes for an hour to an hour and a half along the river trail a couple of times, which was really nice,” Mitchell recalls.

The rides were deliberately easy, simply turning their legs over while enjoying the scenery and wildlife. She also completed a couple of short runs no longer than 30 minutes or demanding.

Her only swim was a brief dip in the river to test the water temperature and a new wetsuit, purchased after her previous one split during a 70.3 race in Leipzig, Germany, earlier in the trip.

More surprisingly, Mitchell wasn’t experiencing any crippling muscle soreness she remembered from her earlier Ironman days.

“It’s strange. They sort of ached, but they didn’t actually feel sore,” she explains.

She believes advances in running shoe technology have made a meaningful difference to how her legs feel after an Ironman. She raced in “super shoes” but suspects recovering from back-to-back marathons would have been considerably harder in the shoes available a decade ago.

Still, there was plenty of uncertainty. When asked whether she questioned the wisdom of attempting another Ironman, Mary laughs: “Oh, I thought about that just about every day.”

“If they’d had a half [Ironman] race, I probably would have dropped down to that distance.”

She reasoned that California’s current-assisted, wetsuit-legal swim would be far less demanding than Kona’s ocean swim. The flat, relatively straightforward bike course also appeared manageable.

But the marathon was another matter entirely.

“My big concern throughout the whole week was the run. Can you do two marathons in eight days with having raced in Kona with the conditions that are notoriously one of the more difficult races that you can do?”

Mitchell had trained specifically for Kona and made no adjustments to prepare for the double. Whatever happened in Sacramento would simply happen.

As expected, the California swim was a very different experience. Thanks to the river current and wetsuit, Mitchell emerged from the water in approximately 55 minutes, effectively halving her swim time from Kona.

But the bike wasn’t entirely without incident. Early in the ride, Mitchell developed significant pain in her quadriceps muscle and her shin. By the end of the first 90-kilometer lap, she was seriously considering pulling out.

“I was thinking, should I stop? It’s really quite sore,” she recalls. “Am I causing damage?”

She decided to continue to the next aid station and reassess, knowing she could stop at any point. Eventually, the pain subsided.

With no expectations, and already holding her Kona qualification for the following year, Mitchell approached the rest of the race with an unusually relaxed attitude. She chatted with volunteers, stopped when necessary, and enjoyed the atmosphere.

“I was just chilled the entire race because I didn’t have anything to prove,” she explains.

The marathon, her greatest concern, proved surprisingly manageable. Rather than experiencing the crushing fatigue she had anticipated, Mitchell found herself settling into a rhythm. The crowds were enthusiastic, the aid stations welcoming, and she passed the kilometers chatting with other competitors.

Her marathon time, 4:23:30, was almost identical to the one she had run in Kona eight days earlier. When she crossed the finish line in 11:32:45, she had not only completed the experiment but had also won her age group again. Andrew had done the same.

“To our astonishment, we both won our age groups,” Mitchell says.

Perhaps even more surprising was how they felt afterward.

“When we first started this sport, you do an Ironman and basically couldn’t walk for three days. Getting up out of a chair was really difficult and painful.”

This time, within 24 to 48 hours, both felt remarkably normal.

Mitchell discovered triathlon in her 30s, partly because Andrew was already involved in sport and she was tired of being left at home while he trained. She bought a cheap bike, started entering local short-course events and quickly fell in love with the sport and its community.

Her first Ironman came in 2004 at Busselton in Western Australia. Like many newcomers, she initially assumed it would be a one-off experience. More than two decades later, she’s still going.

Now retired and living in Adelaide, Mitchell trains up to 20-25 hours per week during her biggest blocks. She has worked with a coach for many years and increasingly recognizes the importance of strength training and nutrition, particularly in preserving muscle mass as she ages. Around five years ago, she also began working with a sports dietitian to improve her fueling, gut training, and overall nutritional approach.

But Mitchell is quick to point out that endurance sport doesn’t consume her entire existence. She enjoys good food, wine, socializing, reading and traveling with Andrew. And while she is competitive, she says curiosity is an even greater motivation.

“I just want to see how far I can push myself,” she explains.

Since retiring, Mitchell has challenged herself to do “at least one thing each year that takes me out of my comfort zone.”

Last year, that meant racing Patagonman in Chile, confronting her dislike of cold water by jumping from a ferry into a freezing cold fjord to start the race. This year, it was the Kona-California double. Next year, she’s already entered the 100-kilometer Tarawera ultramarathon in New Zealand.

For Mitchell, the biggest reward of the double wasn’t another age-group victory. It was discovering that, at age 67, she could still surprise herself.

“I think it resets your mind. It resets your thinking about what your body can achieve. And what mentally you can achieve,” she reflects.

The experience also reinforced what she loves about triathlon: the places it takes her, the friendships it creates, and the opportunities to challenge assumptions about her own limitations.

“It’s taught me that you’re stronger than you think you are, mentally and physically.”

Would she ever attempt two Ironmans in eight days again?

“No. Absolutely not. There’s no need to repeat the experiment!”

For all the satisfaction of the achievement, Mitchell admits she would have liked more time to savor her second Kona world title. Instead, almost immediately, she was packing up and preparing to race again.

“It would have been nice to just chill and enjoy it a little bit more,” she explains. “Have a couple more glasses of wine, soak it in.”

But the experience did change one thing: Despite initially declaring that 2026 would be their last Kona, Mary and Andrew have both accepted qualifying slots to next year’s World Championship.

#8936. COROS Doubled the Price of Its Bike Computer. Can the DURA 2 Compete With Premium Rivals?

COROS kept the feature that made the original stand out and rebuilt nearly everything around it. Now the DURA 2 has to justify its place among other premium options.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The original COROS DURA stood out for two reasons: battery life and price. At $249, it was a (relatively) affordable alternative to the Garmin and Wahoo computers most riders already knew. Just with a solar charging feature that made charging almost optional. But it also felt like the first-generation product that it was. The DURA 2 is COROS’s attempt to move beyond that niche and compete with computers from Garmin, Wahoo, and Hammerhead.

The DURA 2 has a new, unusually slim form factor, a larger 3.5-inch touchscreen, updated maps, and redesigned controls that replace the original’s thumb dial. It also adds voice commands, music controls, and a built-in bike bell. The screen is a memory-in-pixel display, rather than the bright, phone-like panel found on OLED displays on the Karoo and latest Garmin head units. COROS’s priority here is a legible readout while minimizing the power demand of the screen.

Battery life remains the headline. COROS rates the DURA 2 for up to 120 hours in standard GPS mode, or 70 hours with dual-frequency GPS, before factoring in solar charging. After 30 hours of riding with paired sensors, occasional navigation, and the screen at full brightness, my unit still had 77 percent battery remaining.

The price of the DURA 2 has changed along with the ambition. The computer costs $499 on its own, or $549 with COROS’s aluminum mount—a steep jump from the original, though you can skip the bundled mount if you already have a compatible one. The question is whether the DURA 2’s much longer battery life, improved interface, and the COROS ecosystem make it a compelling alternative at this price. After riding it, I think the new DURA is a much more complete and compelling computer. But it hasn’t quite closed the gap to its competitors.

The DURA 2’s memory-in-pixel screen won't win anyone over with vivid colors or smartphone-like detail. That’s fine with me. I don’t use a cycling computer to watch videos or scroll social media. I want to glance down, find the information I need, and get back to riding. The DURA 2 does that well, with arguably the most legible screen in direct sunlight I’ve seen.

The screen struggles most in inconsistent, high-contrast light, such as bright dappled sunlight through tree cover. This is when I wish the DURA 2 offered any kind of meaningful backlight. To my eyes, changing the screen brightness from full to all the way off made no noticeable difference. This wasn’t a huge issue on basic numerical data pages, which stayed very legible, but when you’re trying to discern map detail, it felt a little tough, especially while riding.

Some riders will still prefer the brighter, higher-resolution screens on the Hammerhead Karoo or Garmin’s high-end computers. That’s a valid preference. How beautiful a screen looks isn’t a huge priority for me.

The maps themselves are a big improvement over the original DURA. In my experience, the Hammerhead is still the standard for map legibility and ease of on-device navigation, but the DURA 2 is now quite good. It shows street names at closer zoom levels, and the map responds quickly when you pan or zoom. Both the processing speed and touchscreen response are dramatically better than on the first DURA, and are now close to what I expect from Garmin and Hammerhead.

One screen quirk is that Coros has no way to manually lock the screen. COROS says it will automatically lock when it detects too much rain. I would still like to have a manual lock setting, even if the automatic system works as promised. I suspect COROS could add that option in a future firmware update.

Good riddance to the dial. I gave the original DURA’s dial a fair chance, and it could be useful once I got used to it, especially with gloves. But I also found it clunky and a pain to use while riding. The DURA 2’s new haptic buttons work as advertised, and the touchscreen is far more responsive than it was on the original.

The screen is a little less responsive with gloves on, but not dramatically less than other touchscreens I’ve used. The physical buttons help, and the new layout feels more straightforward. The DURA 2 is simply easier to operate on the bike compared to the original.

The offset Garmin-style mount connection is a small but useful design feature. Larger computers can run into clearance problems with some proprietary out-front mounts. Because the DURA 2’s connection point sits farther back, I’m less concerned about that here. I tested the computer without buying COROS’s optional mount, which I appreciate having as an option because I already have a bin full of included out-front mounts that I couldn’t give away if I tried. Being able to opt out of yet another one was actually kind of refreshing.

I’ve recorded 31 hours of riding on the DURA 2, and the battery is still at 82.4%. That’s with multiple sensors paired, occasional navigation, and the screen at full brightness.

Even with the caveat that battery usage will vary from user to user based on factors like location and use case, the battery performance is extraordinary. If you regularly do rides longer than 20 hours, this is probably the computer to get. No other current head unit I’ve tested comes close to this kind of real-world endurance.

For shorter rides, the advantage is less dramatic but still useful: charging becomes one less thing to remember. And Coros deserves kudos here for maintaining battery-life performance with the DURA 2 while adding a larger screen and more processing power to the unit.

Navigation on the DURA 2 with the updated maps is a clear improvement. The faster processor makes the device feel much less sluggish when zooming or scrolling the map, and the map is easy to read while riding. Street names at tighter zoom levels are a welcome addition compared to what the original DURA offered.

My main reservation is that rerouting still depends on your phone. I get the practical argument: most of us ride with a phone anyway, and the phone can handle it. But it still feels like a shortcoming in a $500 cycling computer. Other units can reroute on their own, and I’d rather not rely on a Bluetooth phone connection when I’ve already paid for a dedicated device.

The rerouting itself is kind of hit or miss. Most of my testing has been in Southeastern Pennsylvania, and so far the DURA 2 (or, I guess I should say, the Coros app on my phone) has sent me down a trail into a stream crossing on my commuter bike only once. Following a route I designed and loaded onto the DURA 2 has gone smoothly, as expected. But I wouldn’t trust the Coros-suggested routes when navigating to a point on a map or when rerouting in an unfamiliar place.

Finally, I personally don’t mind manually loading a route onto my head unit. But in 2026, route sync should be mostly automatic. Hopefully, they can add that in a future firmware update.

Sensor pairing and ride syncing have been trouble-free for me. I’ve had no issues with the sensors I use, and activities push to the app smoothly after a ride. Which is what I expect from a core cycling computer function in 2026.

Structured training is now more than passable. I don’t use my head unit to guide workouts, but I appreciate that COROS has made the feature more useful for riders who do. You can now pause an interval without pausing the ride recording, which feels like it should have been possible from the start, but I’m always happy to see improvements.

The COROS app and Training Hub are also strengths. In some ways, the experience is simpler than Garmin Connect, and I find parts of it easier to use. You can build routes, send rides to Strava and other platforms, and see your training data alongside recovery information from a COROS watch. If you already wear a COROS watch off the bike, that integration is useful. As with Garmin Connect, though, you get the most from the system when you use the company’s hardware.

The new music controls are great, and they’re seamlessly integrated. The electronic bell sounds like an actual bike bell, which is great. But it can’t currently be paired to a bonus button on Di2 or AXS, which Coros can fix in a future firmware update.

The voice control is puzzling to me. Garmin just unveiled this feature on its latest 1060 unit, and I’m just not sure why. I’ve spent 20 years riding without talking to my cycling computer. I would much rather companies perfect their UI and button interfaces so riders can quickly and simply access the functions they need instead of implementing voice controls. I’m sure some riders will find it useful, but I can’t see myself talking to my cycling computer any time soon. Especially since every time I tried to talk to the DURA 2 while riding, it couldn’t understand me, so there's definitely room for improvement.

The DURA 2 is a much better computer than the original DURA. It has a better screen, faster maps, more responsive controls, usable training features, and a more complete app experience. Most importantly, it keeps the exceptional battery life that made the original interesting in the first place.

The price has doubled, and there's really no getting around that. I think the improvements, plus the new form factor, justify an increase. But at $499, the DURA 2 is basically the same price as the Hammerhead Karoo 3 and not much cheaper than the Garmin Edge 850. Both units have their own strengths and trade-offs, but they're polished and fully functional. By contrast, I have written the phrase “hopefully this gets fixed in a future firmware update” three times in this review.

The DURA 2’s biggest strength is that it no longer feels like a budget computer asking you to overlook its rough edges. It feels like a serious head unit with exceptional battery life, and if you regularly ride 20 hours straight, it’s the easy pick. If you don’t, the DURA 2 is still a big step forward over the original, but the rough edges still need a bit more sanding given the jump in asking price.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8935. The 7 Best Jogging Strollers for Every Active Parent

These strollers combine comfort, convenience, and style. They’re perfect for moms and dads trying to get a workout in.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Getting out for a run as a parent of a little one is made infinitely easier with a great jogging stroller. As a running mom, I spent countless hours behind my kids, and now my nieces and nephews lacing up and getting behind a stroller for my own mental and physical health and giving my siblings a much-needed respite (I even bring back treats).

I’ve since made running my job, and have had the opportunity to test dozens of running strollers over the years, and let me tell you, they are not all the same. The range of quality and ride between them can be pretty bananas, and as someone who tends toward higher mileage, it took me a long time to find one that I loved.

Thankfully, jogging strollers have evolved a lot since my first runs with my baby over a decade ago, and now there is a great jogging stroller for everyone no matter your height, running style, surfaces you run on, or miles you’ll be logging. There are strollers that work as both running and everyday strollers, luxury running strollers, multisport strollers that can hit the snow, be towed by a bicycle, or pushed on your own steam, and there are high-tech jogging strollers ready to rack up at the races.

Every year, I dedicate hundreds of hours to testing jogging strollers. I run with kids aged roughly 7 months to 3 years on tracks, pavement, highly groomed trails, boardwalks, and even those charming New York sidewalks. Each stroller clocks at least 40 miles under my watch through all sorts of conditions—rain, snow, sunshine, you name it, we’re out there. Snack testing is a must for cleanability checks, naturally.

Storage? I’ve crammed everything imaginable into the baskets on these. Brakes get a relentless workout. I've folded, unfolded, and hauled these things all over the tri-state area. Airports? Been there, done that (huge mistake, by the way). Here’s my travel tip: check it in a stroller travel bag and thank me later.

Beyond the specs, it’s about the feel. How easy is it to push and steer, even one-handed? And since my nieces and nephews are my precious cargo, their comfort is paramount. We log countless miles, and I see firsthand how happy they are (or aren’t) in each stroller. Some provide a dream ride, others unleash their inner tiny terrors. Basically, I get the real 411 on what works and what doesn't.

Thule makes some of the best tech and outdoor gear on the market, and this stroller is a shining example of the brand. It’s somehow both rugged and elegant, providing the runner with easy, light-touch steering and braking. I was a huge fan of the two previous iterations of this stroller, but this version has surpassed my expectations. I always had issues with the length and size of the canopy, and the tilted position of the seat. But this version sits more upright and has a more generous canopy than its predecessors, making it more comfortable for your little one.

The pneumatic tires are fab and give the stroller a lot of give to glide over difficult terrain like boardwalks, bumpy tracks, and even some trails. I took this beast out on the jankiest boardwalk in all of the land—Rockaway Beach in Queens, New York, and not only did my little nephew fall asleep and stay asleep (and secure) in the stroller even as I almost tripped a dozen times, he fell asleep so deeply that he actually transferred from the stroller to the car seat without a stir.

The storage basket is a decent size, but I do wish it was mesh material, which sand and other dirt could fall through. Also, given that it’s a solid fabric and not mesh, I’d expect it to have a larger weight limit. As it is, 15 pounds is all you can carry beneath. That being said, there are tons of accessories, including handle bags that increase storage capacity and convenience.

I love the twisting hand brake on the Thule. It is a less-abrupt stop than a traditional hand brake, giving you more control. The foot brake is easily operated as well, though disengaging the brakes should not be done in sandals or bare feet.

As for the car seat attachment and available bassinet, both are great, but they do come at an extra price, and the Thule UG3 is bulky for every day. However, it’s such a nice ride, and since the front wheel locks in place and unlocks for easy turning, it is usable as an everyday stroller.

Finding any stroller for under $200 is a feat, especially right now. For families on a budget, the Baby Trend Expedition Jogger is a fantastic option that doesn’t skimp on features. Surprisingly, it includes multiple parent and child drink trays, an accessory often sold separately with more expensive models, adding a bit of convenience. (However, when running, skip the hard cups for the toddlers for safety.)

For the price, the ride is smooth and capable of handling casual jogs and everyday outings. However, it’s worth noting that the overall build quality and components feel a bit flimsier compared to higher-end strollers. The fabrics are a bit scratchier, and the frame and accessories are just not the same.

That said, it’s still a solid stroller with a lot of potential for families. It’s probably not going to withstand the same high mileage or rigorous use as its pricier counterparts, but it’s ideal for those with less intense running routines. Also, it’s specifically designed to be compatible with Baby Trend infant car seats, which is something to keep in mind when considering your overall travel system.

So you don’t want to store a stroller for every occasion? I get it. I live in Brooklyn and understand the limits of small spaces. Enter the solution to your problems: The Guava Roam is a fabulous compact everyday and jogging stroller known for its easy maneuverability and relatively compact fold. It features broad car seat compatibility via its adapters for various brands including Graco, Nuna, UppaBaby, Cybex, Chicco, and Britax. It has one of the smallest footprints both folded and unfolded, and while it’s a bit on the heavy side at 28.5 pounds, the way it folds makes it easy to lug around and stash in your trunk.

But the diminutive size and convenience aren’t the only things that make this an outstanding option for families and runners. My favorite bit about this stroller is the fact that you can lock and unlock the front wheel via a control at the handlebar. It’s genius. I have no earthly clue why more stroller companies aren’t doing this.

I’m also a huge fan of the independent suspension on this stroller that settles and levels as you hit large divots, giving the passenger a smooth, easy ride.

The seat on this stroller is our 3-year-old tester’s favorite, with the five-point harness that’s “not pinchy” and the seat “nice on your booty.” I like the accessory kit near the adjustable handlebar that fits your drink, your phone, your wallet, and at least four mini bags of gummy Nerd clusters (my running fuel of choice).

The stroller isn’t perfect, but it’s so good, you can almost overlook the shallow undercarriage basket and the fact it’s lacking a hand brake. Ideally, I’d love for this stroller to also have pneumatic tires for longer runs and better shock absorption, but the whole thing is just so convenient, its positives easily outweigh its negatives.

I’ve hauled about a gajillion strollers in and out of car trunks, and I know which ones claim to be compact when folded, and which really are. The Cybex Avi Spin is actually a compact jogging stroller. It has a unique way of folding that allows you to either do a basic, one-handed compact fold, or go all the way, and remove the tires first, and then fold it into something that’s around backpack-sized.

The ride is lovely for the jogger, with an adjustable handlebar (it requires two hands to adjust), soft, moisture-wicking grip, and lockable front wheel with an easy deceleration hand brake. It coasts over ruts and bumps really well, but it’s by no means going to hit any trails and remain stable. Jogging strollers aren’t really built for that, by and large.

It cleans up beautifully as well, with removable, machine-washable fabrics, including the UPF 50+-rated canopy. Just pretreat the fabric, wash on gentle, and lay flat to dry.

I do have one gripe, though, and it’s not nothing. The ergonomic, nearly lie-flat seat is fantastic for naps, and the no-rethread, easy-to-adjust harness is great, but younger passengers will lose most of the view if they’re reclined even a little purely because of positioning. This is common on many strollers, but for some reason, is more pronounced on this model. Our tester cared not at all, though, as he was busy looking straight out at the flock of American oystercatchers gathered on the boardwalk at the beach in Queens, New York, where I tested this stroller. My suggestion? Find a running area with dopey looking birds and kids are thrilled. Egrets are also a favorite, I’ve found.

I am a massive fan of this double stroller—Bob gets it right with this one. It’s largely one of the easiest to assemble and to fold, whether or not you take off the wheels. It’s a joy to push, even if you have two large toddlers in the seats. The tires are my favorite of any standard jogging stroller on this list. They are the best aligned, and the adjustable front wheel means you never have to worry if it comes out of alignment, as you can just fix it in a few tweaks.

But oh, how I could write sonnets about the storage. You know what you need a ton of when you’re pushing two kids for a two-plus hour run? Everything. Diapers, wipes, snacks, drinks, extra clothing, sunscreen, snacks for yourself, a few bottles of water, and more. And with the giant storage basket and all the storage cubbies on this beauty, you’ve got the space to hold them. The only thing it doesn’t store is extra patience for when they start fighting at mile 10 and you have 3.1 more miles on your run.

I have run over 200 miles with this stroller, and though I have had to replace the inner tube in the front tire, the stroller is still in great shape. The combination mesh and sealed poly storage basket underneath has seen some things in its life, and it still comes out clean and doesn’t smell, which is a huge accomplishment considering all it has been through.

While lugging it around folded isn't the easiest task, the Bob Revolution 3.0 Duallie’s exceptional performance and ample storage more than compensate. Overall, this double stroller is a top pick for parents who love to run and need the capacity for two little ones. It’s a durable, comfortable, and thoughtfully designed stroller that will make countless runs a joy for both you and your children.

I had heaps of fun testing this stroller out, and recently, I even got on a bicycle (not my thing!) and tried it out in tow mode. This stroller is a beast and, truly, it is only for the most sporting amongst us. If you’re a serious outdoor fanatic, you’ve met your match. It’s designed like a bike trailer, but thanks to its multiple bases/setups, it works as a stroller, a jogging stroller, a bike trailer, and even a stroller on skis for snowshoeing and fun in the sand.

This is technically the double version, but I think it’s worth it to get the wider Chariot Cross 2 over the single version, as it feels a bit more stable than the single, and gives your child some extra space. The seats inside are roomy, and I had no complaints from the Peanut Section about the straps or cushion levels, no matter if the kids were being towed, pushed, or shoved over ice and snow.

Switching the kits out could be simpler, but it’s not especially difficult. I managed to do it pretty easily, and I have a partially paralyzed left hand. Putting it together initially is honestly a bigger pain. It’s easy to clean, though, with removable pads. The materials can take a serious amount of scrubbing and hosing off without showing any wear, which is good considering how filthy a stroller like this could become.

I love the oversized storage bag that affixes to the back. It’s simple to use and clean, and deep enough to fit way more than you’d expect. It’s a slick feature that puts this stroller in a category of its own.

As for the ride, it’s as smooth as it can be over the snow, sand, and ice. This stroller is a bit heavy for an all-out run, but great for jogging slow, easy miles. As a regular stroller, it’s great for myriad applications, but my favorite way to use it is when you’re in a buggy area, as it’s completely enclosed. As a bike trailer, it shines, holding its ground and keeping everything steady. For serious outdoor enthusiasts seeking a versatile and durable multisport option, the Thule Chariot Cross 2 is a top-tier choice that's built to handle almost any adventure.

I’ve pushed the Veer Switch&Jog over 25 miles on all kinds of terrain, and it did well on almost everything. I struggled to push it on mud and sand, but that’s true of just about any stroller. The second I find one that doesn’t? You’ll be the first to know.

My favorite thing about this baby is that you’re able to switch out the jump seat back and forth. Additional pieces are available. The cooler is great, and the booster seat takes about two seconds to set up at a restaurant, which freaking rocks when you think about how dirty restaurant high chairs can get.

During the testing we had a projectile vomit situation. Totally my fault. I overfed the small human treats before the run. My bad, I know better. I took it straight to a self-serve car wash and sprayed absolute crap out of it with the a high-pressure wand. After a little scrubbing, it was totally fine, and the smell came out too (thank god, because it was dairy). I do wish the fabric was machine washable, but it’s attached so firmly to the frame that I get why it’s not.

On runs, it’s stable, and the telescoping handle and handbrake are both easy to use. The front wheel locks for straightaways and unlocks when you’re just wandering around the city.

Folding it is kind of a pain in the you-know-what, not gonna lie. But it’s a convertible tank of a stroller, and it’s very hard to beat at this price.

Given that jogging strollers can be a significant investment, it's crucial to select one that aligns with your needs. To ensure you choose the right stroller, consider these key specifications:

These specs directly relate to your running style. Serious runners will prioritize performance features like wheel type and suspension, while casual joggers might focus on convenience features like car seat compatibility and ease of folding.

To be included on this list, every jogging stroller must meet certain criteria. Key features of a good jogging stroller include a lockable front wheel for safe straightaways at a running pace, excellent build quality for durability, a large canopy for sun protection, and built-in safety features such as a wrist strap, sweat-resistant handlebar grips, and a secure harness system.

And, not for nothing, but they need to feel good when you run behind them. I can’t tell you how many clunkers I’ve tested that made my runs a chore. They need to provide both the runner and the passenger with a comfortable experience. If you’re kicking the storage basket or your hands feel like they’ve become permanently glued to the handlebar, you’re not going to want to use that stroller.

As avid runners who have embraced parenthood, we understand the unique demands placed on jogging strollers. We know that these aren't just tools for transporting children; they are crucial pieces of equipment that must perform flawlessly whether you're engaged in rigorous training for your next marathon or simply navigating the everyday errands with your little one in tow.

For years, the Runner's World team has been committed to guiding runners toward the gear that allows them to achieve peak performance and enjoy their passion for running to the max. This deep-seated expertise extends into our in-depth evaluations of running gear, and jogging strollers are no exception. Our primary objective is to thoroughly test and identify the options available on the market, and to provide informed and reliable recommendations for runners of all experience levels.

When is it safe to run with your child in the stroller?

The general rule recommended by pediatricians is to wait until the baby is at least 6 months old, and has good head, trunk, and neck control. AKA, they can sit unassisted for long periods of time.

What is the best way to clean a jogging stroller?

Honestly, some of these strollers allow you to remove many of the fabrics and wash them in the machine, but for a jogger, it’s kind of a pain. I suggest taking off the canopy, tilting the whole thing upside down and shaking it out before using a damp cloth and wiping it down, and allowing it to air dry. If it’s really gross, hose the thing down, but take off the harness first, as soaking it can reduce its efficacy.

What Should You Avoid in a jogging stroller?

You should be holding your child’s hard sippy cups and snacks and save those for walking breaks. Jogging can jostle, and I’ve seen some pretty gnarly dental injuries on kids who had plastic sippy cup incidents from jogging strollers.

Generally not. Even if they fall within the parameters set by Disney of 31- by 52 inches, I’ve heard of many of them (apart from the Guava) getting rejected at the gates.
