A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Travel well, spend less, keep your FI timeline intact.

Choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

Pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#8921. I Rode My Bike in a Climate Chamber That Can Recreate Almost Any Weather on the Planet—Here’s My Biggest Takeaway

Inside Italy’s Terra X Cube, a Tour de France simulation became a real-world heat test.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I looked into the giant chamber filled with strategically placed bike trainers and couldn’t help but question what I signed up for. The chamber we were walking into is called the Terra X Cube located in Bolzano, Italy, and is designed to replicate conditions from anywhere on the planet. The chamber can recreate a snowstorm on Mount Everest or a heat wave in the Sahara.

Variables like temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation, and altitude can all be controlled from a small observation room just one door over. I knew immediately when I crossed into the threshold of the chamber and the heat hit me in the face that this would be a rough trainer ride.

I was in Bolzano, Italy for an opportunity to participate in this testing in the Terra X Cube as well as tour the apparel brand Q36.5’s headquarters based in Bolzano. The apparel from Q36.5 quickly became my top choice for cycling apparel after getting the chance to test some pieces from their kit for the last few months. Our hot and humid summer in the Northeast gave a perfect testing ground for the Q36.5 Dottore jersey and bibs—and they shined. When a chance to learn more about this brand by visiting their Italian headquarters came up, I jumped on a plane—the opportunity to experience riding in a climate chamber was a special bonus.

Here I’m going to talk about the unique experience of riding in a climate chamber with the heat turned up and my biggest takeaway that you can apply to your trainer riding this season.

The test course and climate were designed to replicate the last section of Stage 2 from the 2026 men’s Tour de France ending in Barcelona. We rode with a custom workout in Zwift and our data was being tracked across the board: SRM cranks to track power, heart rate data to validate fatigue, and CORE sensors to track our heat strain throughout the workout. The room was set to a balmy 97 degrees Fahrenheit.

There was even a tester from Q36.5 in the room with us with a custom jersey. The jersey he wore was effectively two jerseys cut in half at the zipper and straight down the back. He had multiple CORE heat sensors attached around his body to track which jersey design and material was more effective at thermoregulation. One of those jersey designs will end up in a future product.

The ride was supposed to last for about 45 minutes, but our group was the first of the day and ran into some technical difficulties getting the trainers set up. In one sense this was good because we were able to have an extended warmup on the trainers, but the reality meant we spent an extra 45 minutes warming up in the already heated up chamber.

Thankfully, over the last few months, I’ve been doing heat training protocols with my CORE training sensor. I dove straight in with six weeks of active heat training, then I pivoted to strictly passive heat training with my home sauna. While I was absolutely heating up I was relatively comfortable rolling into the ride.

Once we got through our extended warmup we began the proper ride. Effectively we were shooting for an over-under workout that emulated the end of stage two at this year’s Tour de France. I had my CORE temperature data up on the screen and saw that before we were starting the ride my internal temperature was at about 99 degrees. The giant fans at the front of the room would change power to replicate the airflow during climbs versus descents, but at those temperatures it felt like sitting in front of a massive hair dryer.

As we began the official warmup my temperature steadily climbed—according to my CORE sensor I peaked just over 102 degrees. In the middle of the test I looked around the room and everyone looked like they were putting out high effort, even when we were supposed to be sitting in our recovery phase. The heat was taking its toll and our views did not inspire a boost in energy. Staring at the metallic walls while pedaling on our hamster wheel bikes did not give inspiration for an extra push for our final sprint. But as we finished up our not-so-cool cooldown I couldn’t help but think I would do it again.

After our group left the chamber the second group queued up for their turn on the bikes. The technical difficulties were overcome with our group, so they were able to jump straight into the ride after a five-minute warmup. That night we all regrouped to go through the data and we were able to see our data versus the data from some of the professionals in the stage we recreated. My biggest takeaway from the comparison to the professionals was their core temperature data. The professionals we were comparing against showed very little heat strain compared to even the fittest in our group. It’s worth noting the professionals had also already ridden over 60 miles before our route even started—those professionals were extremely heat adapted.

My biggest personal takeaway was how I could recreate this at home. When I talked to someone else in my group we discussed the similarities to this experience and heat training at home. When I do an active heat session at home I layer up in three layers top and bottom, a painter’s suit with the shins and feet cut off (so it doesn’t get caught in the cranks), and a hat or beanie for good measure. My active heat session numbers at home are surprisingly similar to this experience: typically a 45-minute warmup gets me into zone three of the heat strain index in the CORE app and then I spend about 45 minutes in this zone. This shows you don’t need a massive climate chamber to get the training benefits of heat training. Some warm layers, a painter’s suit, a CORE sensor, and a bike trainer can give you the benefits you need to develop this component of training.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8920. How Yoga Brings You Closer to Yourself and the Life You Want

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about yoga as a science and an art first appeared in the January-February 1977 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Yoga is a science, an art, and a technique which spans the multilevel functioning of the individual. It is a science because of its empirical approach, presented most completely by the classic Yoga Sutras of Patanjali at least 1,000 years ago. Science is defined as a methodology which requires empirical proof of its theories; it requires that which proves a theory be easily repeatable by another experimenter if he/she follows the rules of the experiment.

Yoga, by this definition, is indeed a science. Its rules are given in sutra form and the presentation of Patanjali is a “how-to” book of the highest order. The practitioner need only follow the lead of Patanjali in order to have his own personal empirical results. (It is true that the directions are in parts esoteric and apparently illusive; this points out the necessity of having a teacher upon whom the practioner can rely for advice during certain intervals.) In addition to the work by Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika and the Gheranda and Shiva Samhita are references which can explain the science of yoga.

But yoga is an art, too. Individuals have dedicated their lives to the perfection of this art. This does not necessarily imply the production of tangible output such as texts, although these have been produced in the history of traditional Indian thought. Rather, the use of the word “art” in this context implies the movement toward perfection within, the embodiment of beauty as it can be expressed through the human being. If one dedicates his/her life to the art of yoga, this implies a dedication which does not involve merely daily practice numbering a few hours. Instead, it implies a minute by minute practice which spans years, and some believe, lifetimes of existence.

The art of yoga is the practice of yoga on all levels of existence; this means every thought, action, dream, relationship, food intake, sexual activity, occupation, etc., are brought into the wider perspective of observation in light of the individual’s desire to understand the Self. This understanding does not imply intellectual understanding alone. It implies the “living” or the “being” in the Self rather than just mentally knowing about the Self. One can compare this to the experience of being in a hurricane with merely reading about the experience of a hurricane; the effect would be quite different.

One who lives in the Self has come into a wholeness of being, possibly for us all by virtue of our human existence, but available presently to only a handful due a complex interplay of events which, for whatever reasons, has brought them to a newer threshold of consciousness. Thus the art of yoga lies in bringing perfection into action through becoming one with oneself.

Part of the ability to do this lies with the powerful psychological technique of “acting as if.” If one wishes to meditate, one often begins by acting as if one were meditating. As the form of meditation is assumed, the content of meditation begins to be experienced. If one acts as if one loves another, and acts with sincerity and with honesty, often feelings of love toward that person do begin to flow. So with yoga. If one watches and practices as if yoga were an art and the Self were the artist, then this lends validity to the possibility of this being true.

This brings one to the question of technique. Yoga is also a concrete way of bringing about profound physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual changes within the individual. The student is instructed in yama and niyama (basic ethical precepts), in asanas (meditative postures), in pranayama (conscious voluntary control of the energy associated with breath), in pratyhara and dharana (watching and observing the mind), and finally, in dhyana, or meditation. The final experiencing of samadhi (union) cannot be taught; it is both the result of the foregoing disciplines and independent of them. The understanding of this apparent paradox is part of the process of learning about yoga.

Thus yoga can be seen from the angles of science, art or technique. It can be approached as a small practice of one’s life, or as the way that life is lived, a quality which is brought to live which liberates one from the strong bonds of ego.

#8919. The Brooks Launch 12 Helps You Run Fast—and Save Big

This affordable trainer has racing shoe DNA.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Launch 12 is cushier than a racing flat but can handle hard workouts on the track and on the road. The affordable trainer—a bargain buy for $120—won’t break the bank, but it doesn’t feel cheaply made. The Launch has that Brooks touch; the comfy fit that securely locks your foot inside an airy mesh upper.

We included the Launch 12 in our Best Affordable Shoes guide because it’s an excellent choice for runners wanting a designated trainer for fast days. It’s also a sweet, cheaper lower-stacked alternative in a sea of towering, high-cushioned models.

For the runner who says the Brooks Ghost is too bulky and boxy, the Launch 12 could be your sole mate.

I’ve added track workouts to my training this year after finally overcoming my fear of the dreaded all-eyes-on-me oval. It’s fun to go balls-to-the-wall in today’s super trainers and high stacks during speed sessions, but I sometimes desire a more grounded, minimally designed trainer to really test my fitness. The Brooks Launch 12 is that shoe.

Finding out there’s DNA Flash v2 foam in the Launch 12 is like finding an Easter egg in a movie. It’s a callout to the Hyperion Elite 4, Brooks’s premium racing shoe model. The shoe originally had nitrogen-infused DNA Flash v2 foam to pump up your ride before switching to DNA Gold (PEBA, baby) in the Hyperion Elite 5. But it can’t be ignored that DNA Flash v2 was a form of Brooks’s original super foam.

This gives the shoe a firm, snappy ride with plenty of padding for shock absorption. It’s not max-cushioned, and certainly not super trainer height at 35 mm, but it packs plenty of support for hard and long efforts.

“Typically, I’m a fan of the middle ground when it comes to trainers,” said Content Hyper Editor Ashley Tysiac. “I like to have a shoe with enough cushioning that I feel like my feet are supported, but not too much that I feel like my feet are being weighed down by bricks. This shoe was a pleasant break from some of the heavier, maximalist trainers that I’ve tried in the past couple of years. It’s a lightweight shoe that provides a firm ride.

“There’s not a ton of give to the shoe or spring in its step, but I didn’t mind that. The firm, easy ride was something I could enjoy on regular runs, long runs, and even some runs with faster-paced segments in the middle.”

The Launch 12 is built like a track shoe with its narrow, streamlined last. Tester Ricky Snyder said he had no issues with the fit, saying everything was “perfect, no hot spots or cramping in the toe box, no hard or rubbing plastic parts.”

However, Tysiac—and I—found the Launch 12’s midfoot a wee too snug.

“I wasn’t a huge fan of the lacing system,” she said. “No matter how many times I loosened and re-laced my shoes, it always felt too tight through the midfoot area, causing some noticeable discomfort.”

As a runner with wide feet, I couldn’t agree more with Tysiac. Compared to Brooks’s Hyperion 3, which also has DNA Flash v2 foam along a knit upper that hugs your foot, I felt the Launch 12 was much narrower and constrictive. The Hyperion 3 costs $20 extra, and speaking from experience, it could be worth the spending if you have wide feet like mine.

The Launch 12 is a shoe for runners looking to find a cheaper alternative to the more costly speedwork ones on the market, but it’s also for runners who miss shoes pre-super foam. The shoe may have an older midsole version of Brooks’s special sauce, but the ride takes you back to simple days, when a firmly cushioned trainer was all you needed to get in a run.

“I took out the Brooks Launch 12 on a variety of runs, including regular runs, regular runs with pickups in the middle, and long runs. Perhaps the shoe’s best feature that stands out is how light it is, providing a ride that doesn’t feel too bogged down. They felt light enough to rip off some faster-paced fartlek segments during the middle of a regular run, but still supportive enough to make it through a longer run.”

For $120, you’ll find a trainer that can take on multiple workouts. The Launch 12 is a good deal for the runner looking to save.

#8918. 12 Road Bikes Our Editors Would Actually Buy, From $1,200 All-Rounders to Dream-Bike Builds

From budget aluminum builds to pro-level carbon machines, these road bikes are worth buying.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Over the past year, I’ve spent more time on road bikes than any other type. Why? Because, like for many cyclists, taking a road ride is easier than getting out on a gravel or mountain bike. For road rides, you don’t need to drive to the trailhead or the champagne gravel; simply change into your cycling clothes, grab a helmet, and start riding. This makes road rides great for time-crunched workouts or for a quick mental reset.

Today’s road bikes offer many advantages over those from only a decade ago. Aerodynamic frame designs make many road bikes stand out visually; they also help you ride faster and pedal longer distances with less effort. Wide tires (sometimes up to 35mm) and disc brakes (often hydraulic) provide more comfort, better control, and all-weather performance than the skinny rubber and rim brakes of older road models. Many road bikes also feature electronic shifting that changes gears faster, smoother, and with less effort than cable-actuated shifting, and electronic systems typically require less maintenance.

However, road bikes aren’t only for racing, flat-out speed, or fitness; many of the best road bikes prioritize rider comfort and safety. Other great road bikes incorporate features that make them versatile enough for commuting or multi-day trips. Bicycle companies offer several varieties of road bikes designed to meet the riding demands, bike fit needs, budgets, and personal style of almost any rider. Dozens of brands make road bikes for every type of cyclist: from new riders to elite racers, and everyone in between.

We consider most bicycles with slick (or mostly slick) tires, intended for riding on paved (or mostly paved) surfaces, as “road bikes.” These bikes are usually equipped with dropbars, 700c wheels, and narrow tires. You will find two main styles of bikes in the road category. While bicycle brands give categories fancy marketing names, the two groups are best described as “race bikes” and “ride bikes.”

➡️ Race bikes prioritize speed and performance, often with a more aggressive riding position and a stiff feel. Sub-groups of race bikes include aerobikes and lightweight bikes.

➡️ Ride bikes (often labeled “endurance bikes”) can still be ridden fast and are often as light as race bikes. Ride bikes typically use a more upright riding position, and wider tires enhance comfort and control.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillip’s story, “Why Race Bikes Aren’t Real Road Bikes,” discusses this distinction and why we think race bikes aren’t the best choice for most road riders.

Gravel bikes are another popular dropbar bike option, and they share characteristics with road bikes. However, their knobbier tires and frame geometry make them better suited to unpaved surfaces and even some mountain bike trails than riding on blacktop. Read our Gravel Bike Guide for more details on this bike type.

Specialized’s Aethos goes against dominant road cycling trends. Most road bikes feature aerodynamic tube shapes and deep-profile wheels to reduce watts and improve speed, but these details often add weight and negatively impact ride quality. On the Aethos, Specialized concentrated on low weight and excellent road feel—and we love the results. In his review of the second-generation Aethos, Matt Phillips sums up the ride feel: “I’d say it feels like a hyper light, stiff carbon bike, but the feedback is like that of a beautifully tuned steel bike. Which is kind of ideal, really.”

For the Aethos 2, Specialized adds a UDH dropout and a more upright riding position. Plus, the frame and fork now clear tires up to 35mm wide. These updates give the Aethos 2 amazing versatility and add comfort for long days in the saddle. Best of all, the Aethos 2 Expert model (with SRAM Force AXS components) weighs only 15.9 pounds.

The Synapse is Cannondale’s endurance road line. Designed for comfort and versatility, these models feature shorter reach and a more upright riding position than Cannondale’s race bikes. The Synapse 2 combines the line’s core features into a budget-friendly package; it’s a great option for fitness, commuting, or light touring.

The Synapse’s aluminum frame—available in seven sizes from 44cm to 61cm—includes eyelets for adding racks, fenders, and bags. Plus, it fits tires up to 32mm wide. The Synapse 2 comes with tubeless-ready wheels and a Shimano Cues 10-speed drivetrain. Paired with 46/32-tooth chainrings and an 11–39T cassette, the gear range is wider than many road bikes, highlighted by a super-low gear for climbing hills or when loaded up with bags for commutes or bikepacking.

While Cannondale doesn’t equip the Synapse 2 with its innovative SmartSense system (found on higher-priced Synapse Carbon bikes), you can add it later using a downtube adapter to power integrated front and rear lights and rear-facing radar.

When shopping for a road bike, it can be tough to find a decent-quality bike at a good price. Many high-priced bikes are over-equipped for riders. However, low-cost bikes often use off-brand parts, rim brakes, and quick-release wheels.

For $1,200, the Van Rysel EDR 2 AF is a solid bike for the money. It has a double-butted aluminum frame (it fits racks and fenders), a carbon fork, thru axle wheels, and disc brakes. Van Rysel uses industry-standard component sizing (instead of proprietary parts), so you have more options for compatible parts as you wear out components or want to make upgrades.

The launch of X-Lab in the U.S. is one of the year’s biggest cycling stories, and the brand’s exceptionally-priced bikes have created a huge buzz among riders, bike shops, and media. This attention is warranted: the X-Lab models we’ve ridden have performed great—especially for the price.

X-Lab is an offshoot of XDS, a large China-based bicycle company. XDS sells its own models in many regions; it’s also one of the world’s largest bike and frame manufacturers, with a long history producing OEM high-end carbon frames and forks for many brands—including bicycles you may have ridden, seen raced in the Tour, or lusted after. That manufacturing and engineering expertise, along with massive buying power, enables X-Lab to offer its bikes for thousands of dollars less than bikes from almost any other brand.

A great example of this is X-Lab’s AD8. For $4,500, you get: a WorldTour-proven aero frameset, full carbon wheels (even the spokes!), a carbon crank with power meter, a one-piece carbon cockpit, and a Shimano 105 Di2 groupset. The AD8 even has a carbon-railed Selle Italia saddle.

The lowest price in the world wouldn’t matter if the AD8 didn’t ride well. Luckily, it does. The bike’s geometry and road feel are similar to the Canyon Aeroad, another excellent road race bike. In his full review of the AD8, Test Editor Dan Chabanov said, “It looks fast, and it even makes the woosh-woosh sound of going fast. Everything about it screams speed from the moment you get on it. It has the stiffness and jump that a top-end race bike should have.”

Scott’s Addict RC blends lightweight with aggressive geometry that feels better the harder you push yourself and the bike. It’s one of the rare road race bikes that is as confident on fast, twisty descents as on double-digit gradient climbs. And at a little over 17 pounds for the Shimano 105 Di2-equipped RC 30 model, its weight competes with many far pricier road bikes.

The Addict RC’s geometry gives the bike its descending prowess. The bike is low and long—more BB drop, a longer reach, and a lower stack than the previous-gen Addict. The bike is lower and longer than most competitors in the category, so it’s not ideal for riders who need an upright position or like a mellow-riding road machine. But for those who like a spicy ride, it’s an extremely fun road bike.

The words “Pinarello” and “value” don’t typically fit together. However, the legendary Italian brand provides a solid package at a reasonable price with its X1 model.

As Matt Phillips explained in his review of the F7 road racing model, Pinarello’s road bikes are renowned for precise handling and excellent ride feel—as well as high prices and aggressive race-bike fit geometry. Pinarello flipped that script on the X1, delivering an endurance bike for less than a quarter of the price tag of its top-tier models.

Pinarello achieves this price by using some lower-grade carbon fiber and cost-saving component choices. Fortunately, the X1 doesn’t compromise on shifting and braking performance or bike fit. Pinarello equips the X1 with Shimano’s superb 105 12-speed mechanical-shifting groupset and offers an impressive nine frame sizes. However, the bike’s Shimano WH-RS171 wheelset begs for an upgrade to match the frameset’s potential.

When you’re new to road riding, picking the right bike can be challenging since you might not know exactly what type of road rides you’ll enjoy. That’s why bikes with a balanced approach and a good price—like the Specialized Allez—are the perfect choice for new cyclists. And they’re also great for experienced riders looking for a solid bike at a reasonable price.

The Allez provides a snappier ride that transmits the feel of the road in a palpable, yet not overbearing way. It fits wide tires (up to 35mm), and Specialized equips the Allez with Shimano Cues 10-speed components, which feature a wide gear range and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes.

The Allez’s ride feel won’t be confused with its carbon cousins like the Aethos 2 or Tarmac SL, and its handling isn’t as razor-sharp as the Allez Sprint aluminum race bike. However, the Allez is a well-rounded, capable road bike at a great price; it’s sure to please many cyclists.

Trek’s Domane was one of the first dedicated endurance road bikes when it was launched 14 years ago. The recently released fifth-generation platform adds versatility while stripping weight. It did this by removing IsoSpeed from the Domane, a decoupler system which provided vertical compliance over rough terrain, and was the platform’s signature feature.

Instead of building a system into the frame, Trek replaced IsoSpeed with plump, 35mm-wide tires. It’s a simple change that absorbs road chatter and soaks up potholes without adding weight, cost, or maintenance complexities. Wide tires also improve control and traction on less-than-perfect road surfaces.

Trek offers ten Domane models, priced from $2,400 to $15,000. The second bike in the lineup, the Domane SL 5 $2,700 gives you 35mm tubeless tires, a 2x12 Shimano 105 mechanical shifting drivetrain, and hydraulic disc brakes. It’s a solid all-road bike that handles everything from training to commuting, and even some dirt road adventures.

In his review of Canyon’s Endurace AllRoad for Bicycling’s 2026 Bike Awards, Matt Phillips wrote, “There are cheap bikes that are pretty good for the money, and then there’s the Canyon Endurace Allroad, which is the more irritating kind of value because it makes you wonder what excuse everybody else has. At $1,499, this bike has no business feeling this complete.”

The Endurace AllRoad checks all the right boxes for a solid endurance road bike: aluminum frame, carbon fork, 40mm tire clearance, Shimano Cues 2x10, hydraulic disc brakes, and useful bag mounts. The bike provides a quiet, smooth, and calm ride on the road. When the pavement gets rough, Phillips says it is “quick enough to stay lively, stable enough to feel composed”.

Overall, the Endurace AllRoad is a low-priced endurance bike that rides like models costing twice its $1,500 price.

Many road riders love race bikes for their low weight and lively feel, even if they never pin up a number and compete. Cannondale recently launched its fifth-generation SuperSix Evo road race bike. While the new Evo looks similar to its predecessor, it includes several upgrades and refinements that push it to the top of the Best Race Bikes of 2026.

The biggest change for the Gen-5 SuperSix Evo is its refined geometry. Cannondale lowered the stack height by 10mm. This helps riders achieve a lower handlebar height and a roomier cockpit feel. The brand also added a frame size (separate 50cm and 52cm sizes instead of a 51cm), which should help more riders achieve their needed bike fit. Cannondale offers several SuperSix Evo models, ranging from the $5,000 Evo 5 to the 13.8-pound Evo Lab71 SL at $13,500.

While they weigh more than carbon models, titanium bikes have excellent ride feel, great durability, and classic looks. Unfortunately, titanium costs a lot, and it’s tricky to weld. Combined, that typically makes titanium frames cost significantly more than equivalent carbon or steel bikes. However, small Truckee, California-based brand BlackHeart offers amazing-riding titanium (and aluminum, too) bikes at very competitive prices.

As I said in the opening paragraph of my review of the bike, “The BlackHeart Road Plus Ti is the type of bike most dropbar riders actually need. It’s fast and nimble like a good road bike, while also accommodating generously wide tires. Plus, it’s reasonably lightweight, rides incredibly smoothly, and has solid geometry.”

BlackHeart sells the Road Plus Ti as a frameset for $3,499 or built up with SRAM AXS XPLR groupsets starting at $5,799 (for Rival). A bonus of buying from BlackHeart is the brand’s great service and customization; you can change component sizing, pick your tires, upgrade the wheels, or add a power meter to your bike. BlackHeart will even custom-paint your fork practically any color for a $300 upcharge.

The Cervélo Soloist was one of the first aerobikes in the pro peloton and helped bring wind-slicing technology to road bikes. Now known as the S-series, the Cervélo-sponsored Visma-Lease a Bike Pro team has won some of the world’s most prestigious races on this frame.

True to its heritage, the S5 is a professional-level aerobike designed for those who love to go fast. Cervélo’s engineers optimized every shape on this bike so it zips through the air with minimal resistance; you feel the S5’s speed from your first pedal strokes. While the bike is brilliantly quick, it’s also extremely stiff and responsive, so the S5 isn’t your best bet if you value comfort over speed.

The S5 won’t turn you into Jonas, Wout, Marianne, or Sepp, but it does help you have fun trying.

The bikes in this story range from excellent $1,200 all-arounders to high-performance, dream machines priced well over $10,000—and they’re all great bikes. This is what you can expect to get for your money in 2026.

Road bikes priced under $1,200 typically come with rim or mechanical disc brakes and 8- or 9-speed drivetrains. These are great for flat or rolling terrain, but may feel sluggish on long or steep climbs due to their heavier weight and narrower gear range.

Bikes costing $1,200 to $2,000 typically come with aluminum frames, disc brakes, and 9- to 10-speed drivetrains. Many bikes at this price now come with hydraulic disc brakes, which offer improved stopping power with reduced maintenance compared to rim or cable-actuated disc brakes.

When spending $2,000 to $4,000, you often get a bike that looks and rides like a premium road bike, only heavier. These bikes usually come equipped with 11- or 12-speed drivetrains, disc brakes, and a carbon fork. Some models in this price range feature carbon frames.

In the $4,000 to $6,000 range, expect carbon frames and forks, high-end components, and higher-quality finishing. These bikes also offer significant weight savings over lower-cost road bikes. Electronic shifting, upgraded wheels, and carbon handlebars, stems, and seatposts are common, making these bikes feel faster and more responsive.

Above $6,000, you're paying for top-tier craftsmanship, premium materials, and high-performance parts. Road bikes at this price often feature the same frames as bikes ridden by pros in races like the Tour de France.

Finally, don’t forget to account for accessories and gear when budgeting for a road bike purchase. Remember to factor in items like a helmet, shoes, pedals, bottles, and riding clothes into your total price.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8917. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Tracking Your Intervals

Proper tracking and workout structure can lead to success using this training technique.

Whether you’re aiming for a 16-minute or 8-minute mile pace, utilizing a balanced run/walk interval structure makes for more efficient workouts, better fitness progression, and stronger race performances.

It’s not necessarily how fast you’re going, but the intention behind your intervals that dictates your training and racing success with the run/walk method. Your walk breaks shouldn’t feel like a casual stroll through the park, nor should your run intervals translate to an all-out sprint effort. With the Runner’s World program, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, you’ll learn how to best manage your efforts, organize your intervals, and track your sessions.

From nailing your interval durations to finding your preferred training tracker, you’ll discover how to implement the run/walk method consistently into your routine—and start seeing results in your fitness and race performances.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Tracking Your Intervals, we’ll teach you:

While you can use either time or distance to log your run/walks, we recommend starting with time-based intervals, especially if you’re new to running or the run/walk method. You’ll split your running and walking intervals into specified periods of seconds or minutes, rather than distance logged.

If you’re using a training plan such as Runner’s World Start Running or Run Nonstop plan, you’ll gradually increase your run time while shortening your walk time until your walk breaks disappear altogether. But with the run/walk method, you’ll always have walk breaks built in, and you’ll adjust your run interval based on your current goal or race pace.

Notice that no matter your overall pace, you can allot 30 seconds of walking. It’s an ideal interval duration for reaping the recovery benefits of walking without significantly affecting your pace.

As your pace increases, the larger your run-to-walk ratio will become, translating to more time spent running. For example, you may run for two minutes and walk for 30 seconds to hit a 9-minute mile, but when your goal is to shoot for an 8-minute mile, you’ll run for longer (four minutes) to hit a quicker pace.

Instead of focusing on a specific number or pace, use feel to guide your walk intervals. Be intentional with your walks, keeping them brisk but allowing your heart rate to drop and your muscles to enjoy some recovery. Your walk effort should feel significantly less intense than your run portions.

“I tell my runners you should be walking not like you’re looking for sharks’ teeth on the beach or cracks in the sidewalk. You should feel like you’ve got someplace to be, but you shouldn’t get into the race walking motion that you would see in the Olympics,” says Chris Twiggs, chief training officer at Galloway Training.

As you get faster as a walker, you’ll take some of the pressure off of having to run faster to stick with your goal pace. You may also notice more efficient transitions from walk to run, and vice versa, as you improve your speed.

Because run/walk sessions require meticulous tracking, you’ll want to use an interval timer for optimal results. Your smartwatch or fitness tracker may have interval capabilities, but an interval timer is the best tool for accurately structuring your run/walks. Set your run/walk ratios on the timer before your workout, and attach it to your jacket or waistband. The timer will buzz to alert you during your workout when it’s time to run or walk.

If you’re logging your workouts on a fitness tracker or app like Strava, don’t worry about pressing pause during your walk intervals. Keeping the clock going during your entire workout gives you a more accurate representation of your effort, which makes tracking your fitness progress clearer. After each session, write down your total distance, interval ratio, and how you felt during the workout to measure both your objective and subjective progress.

The last component to consider before heading out the door? Shoes. Lace up a pair of comfortable and supportive shoes to power your run/walk workouts. While most run/walkers should rely on run shoes that transition smoothly between intervals, your shoe choice depends on your preferences and experience. Find your ideal shoe by consulting our run/walk shoe guide, curated by Runner’s World gear experts after putting a variety of models through extensive wear testing.

“The main things to look for [in run/walk shoes] are cushioning, support, and durability,” says Carissa Galloway, RDN, certified personal trainer and race commentator. “If you’re just starting out, a shoe with higher stability is important.”

#8916. The Time of Day You Exercise Could Help Control Blood Sugar

Any physical activity is good for your metabolic health, but research says timing it right may have more benefits for your glucose levels.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Although blood sugar control is essential for those with diabetes, it’s also key for maintaining health overall. Research indicates that blood sugar levels can affect a range of physical functions, including hormone regulation, body composition, digestive processes, and even cognitive health.

That’s why keeping control of blood glucose levels is important, and one way to help might include doing moderate- to vigorous-intensity exercise in the evening, according to a study publish in Obesity.

Researchers looked at 186 men and women who were overweight or had obesity and were diagnosed with at least one metabolic impairment, such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Over a 14-day period, researchers tracked their physical activity and glucose levels, along with the time of day for exercise. Morning exercise was defined as before noon, with afternoon exercise between noon and 6:00 p.m, and evening exercise after that.

At the end of the two weeks, those who did more than 50 percent of their exercise in the evening had significantly lower glucose levels compared to those who were sedentary, and better glucose regulation than participants who mainly exercised in the mornings or afternoons.

The effects were especially notable for those who’d struggled with regulating their blood sugar before participating in the study, according to co-author Antonia Clavero Jimeno, Ph.D.(c), researcher in the department of physical education and sports at the University of Granada in Spain.

Although the study participants were specifically chosen based on metabolic factors and sedentary behavior, he told Bicycling that previous evidence has shown that the results might be the same for those without those factors, and who already exercise regularly.

“In fact, the impact of both physical activity volume and timing for glycemic control may be amplified in those with higher activity levels,” he said.

That’s backed up by previous research looking at active people who were assessed for blood sugar changes based on when they exercised. In that study, published in 2022, those who performed moderate-to-vigorous activity in the afternoon had 18 percent lower insulin resistance compared to morning exercisers, and the evening group fared even better, with a 25 percent reduction in insulin resistance.

One factor that was not explored in either study was the role of dietary changes, and this is an area that needs more research, said Clavero Jimeno. Determining whether a strategy like time-restricted eating—also called intermittent fasting—would be helpful or harmful to glucose regulation when paired with evening exercise is a next step, and is already being studied by Clavero Jimeno and his team. (Some research published this year suggests intermittent fasting may have promising effects on blood sugar regulation, at least in those with type 2 diabetes.)

“Dietary intake is, of course, recognized as crucial for glycemic control, and may influence the results overall,” Clavero Jimeno said. “But in the absence of that information, this current study does emphasize that if you want better control of your glucose levels, evening exercise, done at a higher intensity, may be beneficial.”

#8915. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8913. 15-Minute Beginner-Friendly Yoga, No Flexibility Required

Taylor Lorenz—known online as Taylor’s Tracks—is a certified yoga teacher with more than 800 hours of training in vinyasa, hatha, and yin yoga. Here, she guides you through a practice suitable for any experience level with yoga.

No matter how long you’ve been practicing yoga, returning to the basics is always beneficial. This yoga for beginners practice features a flow full of repeating shapes, including forward bends, side stretches, and gentle twists, all supported by modifications and props, if needed, to ensure that the poses work for any body, regardless of how flexible or inflexible you might be.

Listen to your body, breathe slowly, and enjoy the flow.

Keep two yoga blocks or block-like props (think: thick books) close by. These can help you access poses that your body might otherwise object to so that you can still benefit.

Begin kneeling in Thunderbolt Pose. If this doesn’t feel comfortable for your ankles or knees, slide a block beneath your sit bones to minimize the pressure. If it’s still uncomfortable, you can skip this pose.

Come onto your hands and knees with your shoulders over your wrists, hips stacked over your knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

As you round into your last Cat Pose, tuck your toes and sink your sit bones back toward your heels.

Shift your shoulders forward over your wrists. Keep your toes tucked and with your next exhalation, lift your knees away from the mat and reach your hips up and back in Downward-Facing Dog. Think of your body being in an inverted V shape.

Feel free to bend you knees as much as you need to for the pose to feel comfortable along your hamstrings and lower back. You can also place blocks underneath your hands.

Stay here for 3 cycles of breath, pedaling out your feet by bending one knee and straightening the other, and then switching. You can also sway a little from side to side or simply stay in stillness.

Walk your feet toward your hands to come into a Standing Forward Bend. Relax your neck and let your head hang. You can let your hands dangle or rest your fingertips on the mat.

You can also place a block beneath each of your hands. You might want to bend your knees slightly to ease the strain on your hamstrings or lower back.

Inhale and start to lift your chest slightly, bringing your fingertips to your shins and lengthening your spine in Halfway Lift. Keep the back of your neck long and stare straight down at the mat. You can also keep your fingertips on your blocks here.

Inhale to rise as you come to standing, sweeping your arms out toward the sides and overhead. Bring your hands together at heart center in Mountain Pose.

With your next inhalation, reach your arms back toward the sky. Grab your left wrist with your right hand and guide your left wrist up and over to the right in a Standing Side Bend. Feel the stretch along your left side body.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat. Gaze toward the right.

When you’re ready, come back through center before repeating Standing Side Bend and Standing Twist on the opposite side.

Inhale to come back through center, exhale to Standing Forward Bend.

With your next exhalation, step back to Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward Dog, step your right foot between your hands. Lower your left knee to the mat and sweep your arms overhead in Low Lunge.

Use our right hand to grab hold of your left wrist again, guiding it up and over in a side bend while keeping your balance in your Low Lunge. Press through your right foot and your back knee to help find steadiness.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat.

Inhale both arms back to center, palms facing forward. With your exhalation, bring your hands to the ground or to blocks on either side of your front foot. Start to straighten your front leg, sliding your right heel away from you and flexing your right foot in Half Splits.

You can keep your hands underneath your shoulders or slide them forward closer to your feet for a more intense shoulder and side body stretch.

With your next inhalation, come back through Low Lunge. Exhale, Downward-Facing Dog.

Reach your left leg to the sky and repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Step toward the front of the mat and fold forward in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead with your big toes touching or hip-distance apart. With your exhalation, reach your arms alongside your head and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Keep your arms high and begin to draw your left knee toward your chest, foot flexed. With your exhalation, step your left foot back into a High Lunge.

With your right hand, grab your left wrist, and reaching up and over toward the right side.

Inhale to come back through center. Exhale to open your arms toward the right, left arm forward, right arm back.

Inhale to reach both arms toward the sky. Exhale to straighten the right leg, hinging at your hips and folding your chest toward your right leg with your back heel lifted in a less intense variation of Pyramid Pose. Bring your hands to the mat to frame your front foot, your shin, or blocks on either side of your foot. Take 1 full breath here.

When you’re ready, step your left foot up to meet your right in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead. With your exhalation, keep your arms high and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Gently land your knees to your mat and move through hands and knee into a seated position. Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out toward the sides in Bound Angle Pose. If this feels too intense, slide a blocks beneath each knee for extra support.

Stay here, or round your spine and walk your hands forward as you bring your chest toward your toes. Let your body find where it wants to be rather than force the shape. Take 5 breaths in your chosen position.

When you’re ready, move through a seated position to come all the way onto your back in Savasana. Feel free to add blocks beneath your knees for extra support.

Stay here for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Push yourself upright to a comfortable seat. Bring your hands together at heart center, bow your head, and thank yourself for showing up on your mat today.
