#8878. The Top 9 Running Shorts That Prevent Chafing, Store All the Snacks, and Keep You Cool at Every Pace

Our editors tested several bottoms to determine the top shorts for runners.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

As a year-round shorts runner, I’m an expert in the good, the bad, and the miserable when it comes to running shorts. Comfort, potential for chafing, and storage are front-of-mind when I’m shopping for a pair. When runners look for their next pair, there are all kinds of questions to consider: What’s the right inseam to prevent friction? Are the pockets big enough to store my phone, sunscreen, and gels?

For all my hot summer runners and year-round leg barers, this guide is for you. We go over the best shorts that’ll have drawer life well beyond the first fall leaf, plenty of race-day storage for all the gels and gummies, and other features to look out for when shopping for bottoms.

Runner’s World has been testing products since 1966, vetting the best gear for runners so they can train hard, race their best, and enjoy all the other runs throughout their lifetime. Over the course of three weeks, we had our staff test several shorts to narrow down the best men’s and women’s bottoms during their workouts, from trail running to marathon training, from speed to recovery.

The RW team includes runners of varying levels (not all of us have run a 26.2!), ages, body types, heights, and running goals. We considered well-known shoe brands’ offerings, activewear-centric apparel, and lesser-known brands to give you a range of shorts styles and pricing. Our input lends a well-rounded collection of feedback so we can find shorts for every type of runner.

We awarded Tracksmith’s Session Shorts in our annual Gear of the Year, because they have all the essential features, including comfort, storage, and adjustability. The older version had a zippered side pocket that positioned the girth to the front, causing whatever you stored inside to hit your thigh as you ran.

The newest Session remedies that issue, with the girth set to the back. The waistband is also updated; it’s more flexible and has an internal drawstring, unlike the previous Session. The “Session 3.0” is great for training and racing; three rear drop-in gel pockets make fueling easy when you’re hours on the road, and the silky material provides plenty of airflow.

Shop Men’s at tracksmith.com | Shop Women’s at tracksmith.com

The RC Essential 3” is a short made for racing—at a Best Value price. The amount of storage alone makes the RC Essential a winner; individual compartments along the waistband make separating your gels easier (no more caf or no-caf surprises midrun). The four drop-in compartments are complete with a zippered rear pocket for storing discards (though the pocket is large enough to store a phone, doing so results in jostling).

I tested the short and loved the short inseam and split-leg design. The lightweight, quick-drying fabric alone makes these shorts not a distraction, but I can’t help thinking the lack of fabric on my thighs makes me stride better—and faster.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

Runners flock to the cheap Amazon brand Baleaf because its threads are comfy and check all the boxes when it comes to affordable, functional activewear. Take the men’s Running Athletic Shorts: these bottoms are adjustable, breathable, have inclusive sizing, lots of storage, and just feel dang comfy.

“The shorts performed very well,” said a tester. “My first time wearing these was at a local 5K in August, and the shorts did not hold me back in any way. The drawstring made the shorts nice and secure. I carried only my keys in the zipper pocket on the back, and there were no issues there either. I continued running in them on various types of runs following the race and it was more of the same. Great performance and very comfortable.”

Sweat-wicking mesh briefs provide support, while an internal drawcord allows you to adjust the waistband to ensure a secure, nonslip fit. You may need to tighten that drawcord too, since these shorts run large. They also run quite long; if you usually wear a 30-inch inseam or shorter in pants, these are not the shorts for you.

There are two side pockets and one lower back zipper pocket; all are sizable for a phone, in case you’re a thigh phone pocket runner or the more advanced lower back pocket runner.

These Old Navy shorts are at a jaw-dropping price—and our testers were impressed with how they performed on their runs. Even though the inseam is only 3 inches, Assistant Commerce Photo Editor Saba Ahmed reported no thigh chafing on her runs. “These are definitely the shortest inseam running shorts I own and I surprisingly really enjoyed running in these, especially on an almost 80-degree sunny day!” she said.

The elastic waistband has a drawstring for adjustability. The poly-spandex material felt especially breathable, even on very hot days. They also dry extremely quickly. These are Senior Gear Editor Cat Bowen’s shorts of choice to wear on rainy summer days. The only downside with the shorts was the one side pocket. “I was pretty confused about why there was only one pocket on one side,” said Ahmed. “I appreciated that it had a zip, but I found myself trying to find a pocket on the left side as well and then remembering there was none.”

The 2-in-1 short is a divisive topic (like wearing underwear under your shorts), but tester and RW Editor Matt Rudisill said these shorts by Janji felt like running in half tights.

“The tights portion fit very well,” he said. “Not constricting and not loose. They found that perfect middle ground where they’re snug but they didn’t cause any issues (no chafing, sliding around, etc.). The pocket situation was fantastic.”

The Multi Short could very well be our Best for Storage short, as well. The waistband has five compartments for all the gels, gummies, and Sour Patch Kids you crave on your runs. The legs have snug side pockets to store your phone.

Rudisill was delighted to find one of the waistband pockets had an attached S-Biner MicroLock carabiner inside to stash your keys.

For Your Consideration: Ladies, if you want a 2-in-1 yourselves, we also tested the Ciele DLYShort 4” Long Brief 2, which changed Editor Ashley Tysiac’s mind about 2-in-1 shorts.

“Not only were they comfortable for any workout duration or speed, but I never had to worry about discomfort or chafing,” she said. “In a way, they gave me peace of mind. I could throw them on, and knew that they would feel great and perform well, no matter the workout, distance, or pace.”

Have you fallen victim to the dreaded crotch sweat mark postrun? Enter the Bandit Vanisher collection, which promises threads that don’t show sweat.

Both the men’s and women’s shorts have seven waterproof pockets so your phone won’t become sweat-logged, because even though these shorts don’t show marks, they still retain moisture. The cuffs also have silicone grippers so the legs won’t slide up.

“The apparel does exactly as it promises: it makes sweat vanish,” Features Senior Editor Pavlína Černá wrote in her review. “I ran 9 miles in 80-degree heat one weekend and 10 miles the weekend after, and while my skin was glistening, there was not a single sweat mark on my outfit.”

Shop Men’s at bandit.com | Shop Women’s at bandit.com

The Hotty Hot High-Rise is a classic flow short that we love for all kinds of workouts—especially fast ones. The cut is so flattering with mesh panels on the sides and reflective detail in case you’re an early riser or dusk dancer.

We wish there was more room for storage, but the liner stash pocket and zippered pocket on the side provide just enough room to stash keys and a card.

The flat, high waistband has an interior infinity cord for adjusting.

For men, we like the Pace Breaker Lined Short, which comes in five-, seven-, and nine-inch inseams. The short is updated for a comfier fit around the waist and low-bounce hand pockets.

The airy Smartwool Active Lined achieves a miracle you rarely see in short-seamed, flowy shorts: it doesn’t cause chafing. Senior Gear Editor Cat Bowen praised the shorts for their ample storage room, breathable liner, and ability to stay put as she runs.

Bowen reported no bunching or riding up of the leg openings. An added bonus: the shorts launder well without falling apart. And even though you should wash your shorts after a sweaty session (read: bacteria), the liner is efficient at wicking moisture and not gathering odor—so only you know you’re late on laundry day.

Shop Men’s at smartwool.com | Shop Women’s at smartwool.com

While testing the Twilight Short Tights, I honestly couldn’t stop brushing the palms of my hands against my thighs. The textured fabric, a nylon/elastane blend, is ultrasoft.

I wore the shorts during my marathon training and appreciated the storage they provided for fuel and my phone.

Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough was surprised at the Twilight’s generous storage space despite having only three pockets when he tested the men’s version, the Twilight Half Tights.

“Though it may not seem like it at first glance, the Tracksmith Half Tights have great storage capacity,” he said. “Their three pockets (two drop-in side pockets and a rear zippered pocket) look skinny—very skinny. The side pockets are just over 2.5 inches wide, and the rear pocket runs just over 3.5 inches at its max depth. But the secret to the pockets is their stretch. My phone is more than three inches wide, but it was still able to fit in the side pocket.”

Shop Men’s at tracksmith.com | Shop Women’s at tracksmith.com

It’s about comfort and intention. Some runners prefer a bike short (compression or half-tight, as these shorts are also called) to ensure the legs don’t ride up. Many brands add grip tape on the inside of the cuffs to make the legs stay secure.

On the other hand, a flowy short (or loose or relaxed fit) provides more airflow and can come in a split-leg style, which some runners prefer for racing to enhance mobility.

Inseams can be as little as 1.25 inches or as long as 10 inches for maximum coverage. Some runners prefer a longer inseam to prevent the dreaded thigh chafing, while others want as little leg coverage as possible for racing.

To run with underwear or commando is a question RW staff heatedly discusses every so often. The right liner wicks away moisture and doesn’t cause a wedgie or camel toe midrun. If you prefer to run with underwear, who’s to know? But there are some shorts out there sans liner.

Another hot topic besides running with or without underwear: Storing your phone in the thigh or back waistband pocket? If you run with a phone, location is one thing to consider as well as security. After all, no one wants to feel their phone constantly hitting their leg as they run.

Brands are also finally understanding that both men and women need pockets. Some shorts come with 360 waistband storage; others have deep side pockets. Lastly, if you carry small valuables like keys or an ID, you’ll want to consider zippered or envelope pockets over drop-ins.

We included some options for runners on a budget, but we understand our top picks are up there in cost. These shorts are made of durable, sweat-wicking materials that should last you for races and years to come. But we understand not every runner can afford such an investment.

Some ways to make your shorts last longer are washing without fabric softener (you should do this with all workout clothes so it doesn’t degrade sweat-wicking capabilities) and air drying.

How do I prevent my inner thighs from chafing?

If your runs tend to end with chafed thighs, my first recommendation is to try some shorts with a longer inseam. I find that a 7-inch, or half-tight length, usually provides enough coverage to prevent thigh rubbing. Bike shorts with interior strips on the cuffs also help by keeping the legs from riding up.

If you don't like a long inseam, you can also apply Vaseline or BodyGlide to trouble spots, which will minimize friction where you usually chafe.

Is running in shorts in the winter bad for your knees?

As a runner who resists wearing leggings for as long as I can before hypothermia sets in, I spoke with Shane M. Davis, MD, when I noticed how my knees ached on winter runs. Davis, who is a physiatrist of non-operative medicine at Tufts University School of Medicine in Boston, told me that the cold affects the elasticity of your tissues. You may also experience arthritic joint pain as the weather changes due to decreased blood flow.

If, like me, you're adamant about training in shorts when there’s snow on the ground, one way to prevent joint pain is doing dynamic stretches, like high knees and toe-and-heel walking, before your run.

Should I go commando or wear underwear when wearing running shorts?

This is a hot topic at RW HQ: Some shorts have built-in support, but you should definitely try them on before making a commitment. If you're already getting a wedgie before you start to run, they’re going to be a nuisance during a workout.

Some brands make no-liner shorts, so you can wear underwear instead of an attached liner. Alternatively, 2-in-1 shorts offer more coverage like a bike short with a flowy outer layer for added protection.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8877. Dragon Pose Is the Essential Recovery Stretch For Tight Hips and Back

The yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

The low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

Keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

#8876. We Tested 15 Electric Mini-Inflators. These Tiny Pumps Are Fast Enough to Replace CO₂ on Many Rides

From 90-gram pocket pumps to premium inflators, these editor-tested picks make flat fixes easier.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Pumping up tires is a constant of cycling. Whether you’re checking pressure before a road ride, fixing a mid-ride flat on your gravel bike, fine-tuning your air pressure at the trailhead, or topping up tires on your kid’s bike in the garage, every cyclist needs to put air in their bike’s tires

Some riders don’t worry about the exact psi in their tires, but others constantly check and analyze their air pressure, and the latter group may be onto something. In his story, “More Speed and Comfort? The Right Tire Pressure Can Give You Both,” Test Editor Dan Chabanov explains that having the correct pressure in your tires provides more confidence and control on rides.

Small, portable electric inflators have recently taken the cycling world by storm and quickly gained popularity with riders. For several decades, traditional pumps (floor, frame, and mini), CO₂ cartridges, and air compressors have been the go-to methods for filling tires. While mini-inflators don’t fully replace these other inflator types, these small electric units are now finding their way into riders’ toolboxes, gear bags, jersey pockets, and seat bags.

Over the last two seasons, we’ve subjected 15 electric mini-inflators to the same tests. We originally tested 11 inflators in 2025. In November 2026, we tested 4 models (from Cyclami, PDW, State, and Lezyne) and updated our Best Mini-Inflators ranking. A handful stand out for specific use cases or rider types. But these are only a few of the great pumps out there; choose the one that best fits your needs and budget.

With svelte dimensions and a 106-gram weight, the Ultra Tiny is small enough to stash in a jersey pocket, flat kit, or bar bag. Plus, it quickly inflates tires of all sizes to pressure. The AS2’s super-accurate gauge also makes it worth considering for your home shop or carrying in a race-day tool kit. However, the pump runs a little hot.

At the media launch for the Colnago G-5X, someone asked the brand representatives if any inflators fit inside the internal frame storage. That led me to search for options that can fit inside frames. The Cyclami A5S came up in some discussions, so I ordered one on AliExpress to test.

Overall, it’s a solid little inflator that performs well—sub-one-minute inflation times and a 122-gram weight. The rounded profile and placement of the air chuck (on top rather than the side) help it squeeze into many frames’ internal storage doors. Of the five road, gravel, and mountain frames in the office I checked, the A5S fit into four (it didn’t fit into the Cervélo Caledonia).

Several Bicycling editors rely on the Air Rush on rides and at home. Overall, it’s a solid and dependable pick. It has a nice display, runs cool, and inflates road and gravel tires in under a minute. It also filled five road tires; that’s better than most units. I only wish it were slightly smaller for carrying in a seat bag or internal frame storage.

Like many RockBros products, this mini-inflator isn’t the best at any single thing, but it does everything pretty well overall. It gets tires up to pressure in under 50 seconds, doesn’t run too hot, isn’t too loud, and isn’t super heavy.

The most expensive model in our test, the Ultimate, lived up to its name, hype, and steep price tag. And matching its durable appearance, this inflator is a beast—it gets tires up to pressure in under 30 seconds and inflates eight tires on a single charge. I tested Silca’s claim that the Ultimate will seat tubeless tires—surprisingly, it succeeded.

The Ultimate was the quietest inflator in our testing and tied for the second-lowest temperature. Other than price, the biggest negatives are the Ultimate’s weight and size. One note: after almost a year of frequent use, an O-ring inside the pump failed. However, Silca offered to replace the unit under warranty.

The Pocket SE doesn’t feature a display or gauge, but at only 90 grams, it weighs less than a single CO₂ cartridge and head. And though it takes roughly a minute to inflate a tire to full pressure, I can fill four tires on one charge. The Pocket SE’s one downside is that without a pressure gauge or a 72 psi cutoff, I’d be cautious using it on hookless tubeless road wheels.

For a year, I’ve carried the Pocket SE in my seat bag for flat fixes, and it has gotten me out of plenty of jams. My only complaint is that the button activates easily; a bump or pothole can trigger the unit if it isn’t carefully positioned in your bag.

Portland Design Works makes well-crafted, usable gear for everyday cyclists. The brand doesn’t take itself too seriously, and its products sometimes have whimsical or quirky elements (like its water bottle cages).

PDW’s Essentials inflator follows this mold—it’s well-designed, looks good, and functions well. The Essentials inflates tires quickly, and the gauge is pretty accurate. Its best feature is presets for different bike types (labeled road, gravel, mountain, and city). You can use these to set your tires for your quiver of bikes, or program them for different rides, wheelsets, or riders in your house.

The screw-on chuck is slightly tricky to use and leaks some air if not fastened correctly. While the unit’s body doesn’t run hot, the hose’s base certainly does: heed that yellow warning tag.

Mini-inflators are pint-sized electric air compressors. Larger electric pumps have been around for many years and are commonly used at home, in the garage, or the workshop. Some people carry electric pumps in their vehicles to air up car or truck tires and fill inflatable rafts or SUPs. Cordless air inflators have been a common sight around World Cup mountain bike team paddocks and cyclocross pit zones for several years.

Yet cyclists only started using these inflators within the last three years, when the prices dropped, the form factor shrank, and battery life increased. Riders soon found electric inflators perfect for the garage or the trailhead. Plus, their smaller size makes them much easier to toss in a bike bag or luggage than a floor pump when flying with a bike.

Several cycling equipment brands have released models tailored to bicycle riders’ tastes and preferences. Some companies have even cut enough weight and reduced the proportions to make electric mini-inflators a viable option for carrying in a jersey pocket or flat kit on rides.

The current crop of bike-specific mini-inflators can be broken down into two groups:

1) Small enough to bring on a ride, and 2) Everything else.

Of course, your definition of “small enough” might vary greatly from another cyclist’s. If you ride with a bar bag or frame pack, an inflator like the Portland Design Works Essentials or Trek Air Rush might be sufficiently tiny. However, if you carry everything in a ride wallet or obsess about weight, even Silca’s 112-gram Elettrico Micro might be too large for you.

For our testing, we focused on mini-inflators sold by cycling-specific brands and ones marketed for bicycle use. This isn’t an exhaustive test of every inflator available; instead, it provides context to help you choose one best for your needs.

In two years of testing, we’ve evaluated fifteen models across a wide price range ($15 to $160). These include mini-inflators from respected cycling brands, options from smaller companies, and those that fly under the radar.

To test if size matters, I picked some based on their tidy proportions and low weight. I also chose a couple of larger, heavier options to see whether they push air significantly faster or fill more tires than other mini-inflators. I also bought the cheapest mini-inflator available on Amazon ($14.90 on the day I was shopping) to test it against the pack and see if spending more on a pump really matters.

As with other Bicycling head-to-head product tests (like insulated water bottles, flared handlebars, and wide road tires), we evaluated electric mini-inflators based on real-world requirements, not intricate lab tests. Riders can replicate at home without much fancy equipment.

We inflated the tires to air pressures for a 180-pound cyclist riding a road, gravel, and mountain bike in average conditions (as recommended by Wolf Tooth’s app). For road riders, we recorded the time to inflate a 28mm-wide tubeless tire to 65 psi. We also measured the time to reach 30 psi on a 45mm gravel tire. For mountain bike riders (or folks riding new-school gravel bikes), we clocked the time to 20 psi on a 29x2.3-inch tire. To evaluate the pumps without built-in gauges, we measured the pressure they reached after 50 seconds.

After timing inflation speeds for each category, I fully recharged all devices. The next morning, I tested how many times each electric mini-inflator could fill a 28mm road tire to 65 psi from fully flat. To prevent overheating, I let each inflator cool down for ten minutes between fills.

In addition to real-world tests, we also measured three common concerns of electric pump buyers: Temperature, noise, and gauge accuracy. For these tests, I borrowed equipment from my colleagues on the Popular Mechanics test team.

This included a specially designed fixture that measures bike pump gauge accuracy. Gauge accuracy is important, especially for riders using hookless tubeless road wheels. Since the maximum allowed pressure for these wheel systems under ETRTO standards is 5 bar (72.5 psi), you don’t want to risk a tire blowing off a rim due to a wildly inaccurate pump reading.

Like other users, I have personally experienced noise and heat build-up issues with electric mini-inflators. Early one morning at Sea Otter Classic, my inflator woke the cyclist in the hotel room next door—my sincere apologies to him! Later, on an All Bodies on Bikes group ride, the inflator I borrowed from another cyclist to change a flat melted the plastic valve of my spare TPU tube.

Lesson Learned: Due to excess heat, always use an extension hose when filling plastic-valved tubes with an electric mini-pump.

“Do I plan to carry this on rides?” you ask when purchasing a mini-inflator. If you answered “yes”, look for lighter-weight and smaller-profile models. If you only plan to use the inflator at home, at the trailhead, or at races, don’t focus on size or weight.

Unless you only need to get out of a jam on the side of a road or trail, look for models that fill more than two tires. This allows you to adjust tire pressure and inflate tires on other bikes or spare wheels (and for friends to borrow before a ride—because you know they will need it).

After evaluating these mini-inflators, my key takeaway is that price doesn’t exactly make it the best for your needs. The most expensive pump in our test has brilliant inflation speed, is the quietest, and doesn’t run hot—plus it fills lots of tires. But it’s too heavy and large for most cyclists to carry on rides. However, spending more doesn’t guarantee better performance either, as some pricier models didn’t outshine the low- or mid-priced models. And, as I found out from testing, you probably don’t want to buy the absolute cheapest possible option either (luckily, this model is no longer available).

Skimming listings for different devices, you’ll notice (from similar design details and parts) that a select few vendors manufacture many electric inflator models for every brand. But even if a mini-inflator shares the same outer silicone protector, case, buttons, or display, it doesn’t mean they’re identical. For example, in our testing, the Rockbros model outperformed the extremely similar-looking Muc-Off Air Mach pump.

Unless you specifically need a lightweight, compact mini-inflator for on-the-bike use, spend a little more for a model with a built-in gauge. A display is super handy, and you can pre-set your desired pressure within 1 psi (some even read to tenths).

Pro Tip: If you buy an inflator without a built-in gauge, time how long it takes to reach your optimal ride pressure from fully flat before bringing it out on the road or trail. Then, when you’re airing up a flat fix, you can count off (or use a timer) to get you relatively close to your riding pressure.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8875. Just One Drink Can Make Your Next Workout Feel Harder. Experts Outline a Simple Strategy to Help You Plan Ahead.

How to protect your sleep, hydration, and recovery before a demanding effort.

When you have a big workout or long run coming up, you probably think through your usual checklist, like your fueling and hydration plan, what you’re going to wear, and the route you’ll take. But if you have a drink in the days leading up to that effort, it’s worth considering how it might disrupt your preparation, too.

Alcohol can affect your sleep and your hydration—two things your body relies on to recover from training and prepare for the miles ahead. And while the severity of its effects varies from person to person, even one drink can negatively affect an upcoming workout.

Now, this doesn’t mean you have to give up every happy hour or celebration during a training cycle. But if you want to feel your best for every workout on your plan, it helps to think ahead.

Sports dietitian Pam Nisevich Bede, RD, CSSD, previously told Runner’s World she recommends avoiding alcohol for at least two days—ideally three—before a key workout, long run, or race. Without that buffer, you may find yourself feeling sluggish and under-recovered when it’s time to tackle your important effort, even if you prepared well in every other way.

Even if you think a drink might help you fall asleep faster, Bede explains alcohol actually disrupts your sleep quality. This is a concern for runners because sleeping well gives your body valuable time to recover from the training you’ve already done so you’re prepared for what’s next. According to research, just one drink within an hour of bedtime could reduce rapid eye movement (or REM) sleep, which supports functions including memory and focus. If your sleep is disrupted, you may wake up feeling tired and less ready to take on the workout you planned.

Alcohol will also affect your hydration status before a run as it increases urine production, explains Ron Maughan, PhD, an honorary professor at the University of St. Andrews whose research includes alcohol’s effects on athletic performance and recovery.

Going into a long run or workout dehydrated can make it harder to perform your best, and therefore lessen the effectiveness of a workout.

These effects of alcohol don’t look the same for everyone, though. Maughan previously told Runner’s World that a small amount may have little effect on one person and a much bigger effect on another, so giving yourself more of a buffer is always a safer bet.

Bede’s recommendation is a practical way to make sure you fully recover before a key effort. Not every runner will feel fully recovered after a set number of hours post-drink, but adhering to the two-day rule can help you avoid stacking a night of drinking too close to a run you want to prioritize.

If you’re training for an upcoming race, you’ve probably already got a calendar with all of your workouts planned out day by day. You can use that same calendar to make decisions about drinking.

Start by identifying the efforts that matter most in the coming week. Maybe it’s a long run, an advanced tempo workout you’ve been building toward, or the race you’ve had circled on your calendar for months. Then work backward, aiming for at least two alcohol-free days before that effort—and three if you can.

The idea is to make the choice before you’re staring at the menu and trying to calculate whether a drink will affect tomorrow or the next day’s workout. And if you’re in a particularly heavy training block and hoping to perform at your absolute peak, Bede suggests considering a longer break from alcohol altogether.

If you do choose to have an adult beverage, Bede also recommends taking in additional fluids and electrolytes alongside the alcohol. Proper hydration won’t cancel out alcohol’s effects, but it will help support your recovery. And when an important run is approaching, that two-day buffer after a drink gives you one more way to show up ready to perform your best.

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. #8874. Your 2027 Gravel Calendar Starts Here: 5 Events Worth Planning Your Season Around

Five standout gravel events with epic routes, big vibes, and reasons to train all winter.

On a recent gravel ride one of my riding buddies was telling me that he is beginning to feel like he is falling into a rut with his riding. It’s the same ride from his house during the week and the same group ride on the weekends. I told him that one of my favorite ways to get out of a rut is to sign up for an event. With so many events out there it can be hard to figure out which one to pick.

Gravel has been a growing category for years and looking through the gravel events around the US can feel like you are falling into a doom scroll. When figuring out which one to pick it can be overwhelming because there are so many grinders, group rides, and gravel fondos to choose from.

Signing up for an event a few months out can help get you out of a rut by giving you a goal to strive for. Maybe you add strength training over the winter or maybe you do those zone two rides you ignore. Either way finding the right event can reinvigorate your stoke for riding, especially rolling into the winter.

We gathered a small list of rides from around the country to make it easier for you to set up your gravel calendar for 2027. Whether you want to ride in the mountains of Colorado or the plains of Kansas we have a route for you.

Note: Gravel is ever-growing and changing. As such, entry fees and festivities can change year to year. You can generally expect some free schwag like socks, a tee, or a hat with your entry fee, as well as complimentary food, beverages, and event celebrations. Some events are also affiliated with charities and donate a portion of the entry fee to those causes.

Held during late winter deep in the red-dirt country, The Mid South is a tough challenge to prepare for. It could be a sunny, warm, beautifully leg-searing ripping fast day or a freezing, rainy, slick, sticky, gloppy death march for 100 miles. It all depends on what mother nature has in store. As one of the iconic events on the gravel calendar, it attracts a deep field of pros and recreational riders looking to test their fitness and tune-up for the season ahead. Rain or shine, riders are rewarded with a huge, welcoming community in downtown Stillwater, shared camaraderie with more than 3,600 registrants, and finish line hugs from the event’s passionate and animated promotor Bobby Wintle.

This amalgamation of a gravel grinder meets enduro features nearly 60 miles and 8,000 feet of elevation over gravel roads and sometimes sketchy singletrack trails. The organizers crown the winner based on performance on a handful of shorter, timed segments within the ride. So, you can stop and Instagram the massive views of Mt. Shasta and the Eddy Mountain Range and enjoy all the food and beverages at the aid stations. Though this is billed as a gravel race, the course goes through the Gateway Trail network—a popular mountain biking destination in the area—so you’ll find yourself on singletrack with berms and slightly techy rock gardens. This event is for you if you love ripping singletrack on drop-bar bikes.

Note: Grinduro has expanded to other locations around the world, including Wales, the U.K., Italy, Switzerland, Japan, and Australia.

Known as the Super Bowl of gravel, the 200-mile Unbound (formerly DK200) event is undoubtedly the granddaddy of the gravel scene. Its reputation for being brutal is well earned. The Flint Hills are endlessly rolling and covered in sharp, often chunky gravel. It can be extremely windy, stiflingly hot, and covered in sticky peanut butter mud. It is a badge of honor to finish this sinister double century before the 3 a.m. cut-off time.

There’s a lottery to get in due to the popularity of the event and it just opened up. Throw your name in that hat now with drawings to be announced on November 21. With the entire town joining in the celebration of gravel, it’s something to behold.

You’ll find a star-studded deep pro field leading the charge of this challenging high-altitude course, as one of the hallmarks of the race is generous and equal payouts for men and women. The 108-mile main event features 8,189 feet of climbing. The sweeping vistas of the surrounding mountain ranges, lakes, and ranches take the sting out of the long, exposed climbs. The terrain ranges from fast hard pack to soft, sketchy moon dust, and it includes one long, chunky road right at the end. Steamboat is located at 6,900 feet of altitude, and the course tops out at about 8,200, which riders from sea level will undoubtedly feel.

This event in the northern area of Pennsylvania doesn’t have the alpine views of Steamboat or the prestige of Unbound. What it does have is exactly what the name implies—seemingly endless climbing. This year I completed the 115 mile route and I was impressed that we were on very small bits of paved road throughout the over one hundred mile course. When I talked to the organizer, David Landis, after the race he said the area has even more gravel than he can include into any of these loops.

One tip if you are going to go for any of these distances—bring your climbing legs. Whether you choose the 115 or the 430 mile routes you’ll be getting close to the golden ratio of climbing to miles. If you sign up for the race you need a GPS device (like a Garmin InReach) that can be used to live track the ride.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. #8873. Our Prehistoric Ancestors Were Built for Endurance. In Today’s Increasingly Sedentary World, Could You Outrun Them?

Experts explain the connection between evolution and our marathon potential.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Modern life has made movement optional like never before. ASICS research found that respondents around the world reported spending 86 percent of their waking day not moving. Yet our bodies were shaped by a very different world, where walking, carrying, and running were part of everyday survival.

Around two million years ago, our ancestors began developing a body equipped for endurance running. These adaptations helped them keep moving over long distances. We inherited that capacity, but modern life gives many of us little reason to use it.

A marathon puts that evolutionary inheritance to the test, with modern training, nutrition, and technology helping runners explore their limits. So how would we perform lined up against the ancestors who helped shape us? Could a recreational marathoner outrun Homo erectus?

Unlike other mammals, “humans aren’t especially good sprinters, but we are highly effective endurance athletes,” says David Raichlen, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Southern California.

Some two million years ago, our ancestors Homo erectus lived as hunter-gatherers, spending long periods walking, tracking, and chasing food. “Around the same time, they began to develop some anatomical features that improved their ability to run for long periods,” Raichlen says. “These features include long legs, relatively short toes, long Achilles tendons, a large gluteus maximus, and other traits that help to stabilize the head and trunk while running.”

Our ability to sweat profusely may also have given early humans an advantage in hot conditions, allowing them to cool down and keep moving while other animals overheated.

One popular explanation is persistence hunting: chasing prey over hours until it collapses from heat exhaustion. Professor Lewis Halsey, of the University of Roehampton, says the evidence has become more nuanced. His own research comparing humans and horses supports a human heat-endurance advantage. Humans are less adversely affected by rising temperatures than horses, although horses remain faster. Human success, he suggests, may have come from combining a modest heat advantage with pacing, tracking, cooperation, and a large brain for tactics.

Some internet speculations suggest Homo erectus could run a marathon in around 3 to 4 hours. If the estimate were taken at face value, even its slower end would beat today’s average marathon time of around 4:30 (4:17:00 for men and 4:43:00 for women, according to Running USA’s Industry Insights report from 2023). But where did the Homo erectus marathon time come from?

It remains unclear. One study, focused on time rather than speed and published in the 2020 Journal of Human Evolution, offers a different measure of endurance: its model estimated that Homo erectus would reach a dehydration limit after 5.5-5.7 hours of persistence hunting without drinking, under the conditions examined.

Raichlen cautions against putting a time on possible speed. “I would not say that we know Homo erectus ‘could run a 3:30 marathon’,” he says. “The stronger conclusion is that around two million years ago, humans had evolved a body capable of surprisingly impressive endurance running.”

Halsey is blunter. “Inferring a marathon time from some bones is pushing it,” he says. Many adaptations associated with running are also useful for walking, and they tell us nothing about VO2 max or lactate threshold—key determinants of distance-running performance.

Mac Cassin, Principal Sports Scientist at Wahoo, says the modern comparison needs similar care. “It’s highly unlikely that an ancient human ever set out to run 26.2 miles aiming for a new PB,” he says.

Here’s the real story: we haven’t become biologically weaker, but we have removed the need to move. “The difference between ancient and modern humans really comes down to what is done on a daily basis,” Cassin says. “Overall, human endurance potential hasn’t changed from ancient times to now. What has changed are the physical demands of daily life.”

Hunter-gatherers did not exercise constantly, Raichlen says. Rest was always part of human life. The difference is that movement was embedded in it.

“Acquiring food, travelling between locations, carrying things and performing other daily tasks required physical activity,” he says. “Whereas now modern humans can work, shop, travel, eat, socialize and entertain themselves without needing to move very much at all. The ability to largely remove movement from daily life is a very new concept.”

The consequences extend beyond fitness. Low physical activity is linked to poorer cardiovascular and metabolic health, Raichlen says, while movement also supports mood, cognitive function and long-term brain health.

We may never know whether you could beat Homo erectus over 26.2 miles; what we do know is that our endurance has deep evolutionary roots, and we have our ancestors to thank for the ability to line up at a marathon starting line.

The more useful question is how much of the endurance capacity you inherited you are putting to use. “The more interesting comparison is that modern humans retain an impressive endurance capacity that evolved in a world where regular movement was unavoidable,” Raichlen says. “Today we have largely the same biological capacity, but we live in environments where movement can be almost entirely optional.”

Cassin believes many recreational runners underestimate what consistent movement can achieve over years. “With the correct training, our body is remarkably adaptable,” he says. “The caveat is that adaptation takes time.”

Raichlen advises runners not to treat running as the only movement that counts. “Walk places where you can, take the stairs, get outside, carry things and find reasons to move between workouts,” he says. “A 45-minute run is great, but it doesn’t mean the other 15 waking hours are irrelevant.”

#8872. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Mr. Money Mustache April 8, 2023, 6:43 pm

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

Very accurate, MMM! I’ve got a good friend who works for whatever they call the “water” department of the city of Mesa (right next to Tempe), and whenever I bring up the metro Phoenix water supply issue, he basically says “we’ll be fine, but things will have to change with respect to agriculture in the southwest and lawns/golf courses”.

I worried about it for years, but a bit of research and several articles in the NYT helped calm me down. Here’s one: https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/05/22/climate/colorado-river-water.html .

TLDR: We’re going to have to continue to evolve what we raise/grow/eat to balance the demands on our planet, especially considering climate change (to the surprise of practically nobody reading MMM)

It’s FEWER cars, not LESS. Fewer is used when referring to things (people, cars, buildings, bottles of beer) that can be counted separately. Less is used when referring to things (sugar, coffee) that come in bulk.

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

You'll need 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. Check your current balances across:

Decide your primary transfer source before you need the points. If you're using Capital One, initiate the transfer 5–7 days before you want to book to give yourself buffer time.

If you don't have a Privilege Club account, create one at qatarairways.com/privilege-club — it's free and takes minutes. Once you have your account number, you can link it as a transfer destination in your Citi, Capital One, or Marriott account.

Once you've confirmed availability and are ready to book, log into your credit card rewards portal and initiate the transfer to your Qatar Privilege Club account number. For Citi, this will post instantly. For Capital One, monitor your Avios balance over the next 2–5 days.

Return to qatarairways.com, log into your Privilege Club account, and book the award using your Avios balance. Have your passport and payment method ready for the taxes and fees. Confirm the aircraft type one final time at booking to ensure you're on a QSuites-equipped aircraft.

If you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Also try ±3 days on either side of your target dates — availability patterns are uneven. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

British Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Let's build a real booking so the numbers stop being abstract.

The Route: New York JFK → Doha DOH on Qatar Airways, Boeing 777-300ER, QSuites Business Class.

Cash Price: A one-way QSuites ticket on this route runs roughly $5,000–$8,000 depending on timing and booking window. For a couple, you're looking at $10,000–$16,000 in cash — a number that probably makes the FI-minded reader physically uncomfortable.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

You arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

Dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

This is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.

Do this: Book at the 361-day mark with precision. QSuites availability is genuinely scarce. The readers who get this redemption are the ones who treat the booking window opening like a product launch. Set two calendar alarms — one for 362 days out as a reminder, one for 361 days out as a launch signal. Have your Privilege Club account open and your credit card details ready.

Do this: Confirm the aircraft before you transfer anything. Not every Qatar flight uses QSuites. Qatar operates multiple cabin configurations on its fleet, and even the same route can have different aircraft depending on the day. Always verify the aircraft type (Boeing 777-300ER or A350 with QSuites) in the booking flow before initiating a points transfer. Booking "Business Class" on a non-QSuites aircraft is a common and painful mistake.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou Points as your primary transfer partner. The instant transfer speed from Citi is a real operational advantage. When you find availability, you can transfer and book in a single session. With Capital One's 2–5 day transfer window, there's a risk the seat disappears before your Avios post. Prioritize earning Citi ThankYou Points if this redemption is a goal.

Do this: Add a Doha stopover. Qatar allows stopovers in Doha on award tickets. If your ultimate destination is beyond Doha — whether that's Asia, Africa, or the Indian subcontinent — building in a Doha layover costs nothing extra in points and gives you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, which is worth experiencing on its own terms.

Avoid this: Using Marriott Bonvoy as your primary transfer path. The 3:1 ratio means you need 225,000 Bonvoy points to get 75,000 Avios. Marriott points are valuable for hotel redemptions — burning them at a 3:1 ratio for airline miles is rarely optimal unless you have a massive surplus.

Avoid this: Waiting for a sale or hoping for better availability. Qatar doesn't run award sales. The award chart is fixed, and availability only decreases over time on popular routes. The readers who say "I'll book when something comes up" are the ones sharing their story about the year they almost flew QSuites.

Remember: Miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your Privilege Club account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every 36 months. A single small transaction resets the clock.

This redemption is purpose-built for the ChooseFI couple or family who has spent a year or two being intentional about travel rewards and is ready to cash in on the premium cabin experience they've been building toward. If you and a partner each hold a Citi Premier or Capital One Venture X and have been putting real spend on those cards, 150,000 combined points for two QSuites seats is a realistic 12–18 month accumulation target.

Minimum points required: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. For a couple, plan on 150,000 Avios. Have this balance confirmed before you begin the booking process.

This redemption earns a **Moderate** difficulty rating, and that's honest. The value is a 5/5 — there is almost no better use of transferable points in the entire loyalty ecosystem. But you'll earn that value. **What makes it hard:** First, **availability is legitimately limited.** QSuites seats don't sit open for weeks. Qatar releases a constrained number of award seats, and on popular routes, they go fast. This isn't a system you can approach casually. You need to search early and book decisively. Second, **the booking process has multiple steps.** Unlike a straightforward Chase Ultimate Rewards hotel redemption, this requires confirming availability on one platform, identifying points across potentially multiple credit card programs, executing a transfer, and booking on a separate airline's website. Practice the search so you know exactly what to look for. 3. **Use Qatar's own website for searching**, not third-party tools — Qatar award inventory is most accurately displayed on qatarairways.com. If you've successfully booked a domestic partner award before, you can absolutely do this. The moderate difficulty reflects the preparation required, not insurmountable complexity.

Log into your Qatar Privilege Club account and search for business class award space on your desired route. Look for flights showing QSuites availability — check the aircraft type (A350-1000 or 777-300ER with QSuites). This confirms what BA Avios can book since both programs are in oneworld.

Not all Qatar 777s have QSuites. Check SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to confirm the specific aircraft configuration. Routes to major US gateways (JFK, IAD, ORD, IAH, LAX, DFW) typically operate QSuites-equipped aircraft.

Once you confirm availability, transfer the required Avios from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), or Bilt (1-2 days). Transfer only after confirming space.

Search for the same Qatar-operated flight on ba.com using your Avios. If the flight appears, book online. If you cannot find it online, call BA Executive Club to book partner award flights — agents can see availability that may not display on the website.
