#8870. How to Address Common Causes of Knee Pain While Cycling

Identify common reasons your knees may hurt while riding, and what to do about it.

As a cyclist, you probably know that you should always listen to your knees and the messages they send when they’re not so happy. These messages show up as aches and pains, and they’re common among those who ride. While research suggests cycling can actually help you avoid knee pain later in life, other studies indicate it still affects about 15 to 30 percent of cyclists.

Fortunately, the culprit is often an easy fix, but the first step is to identify what may be causing your knee pain. For example, you may be overtraining and pushing your body harder than it’s used to, straining your connective tissues and causing inflammation and pain.

Any spontaneous twinges of crank-stopping knee pain may feel like they come out of no where, when actually they’re just the first noticeable symptoms of a long-brewing problem. This generally stems from equipment and/or bike position issues, says bike-fit specialist Michael Veal of BikeDynamics in Warwickshire, England.

“Many cyclists are forever tinkering with their position, looking for that elusive perfect position,” he says. But what feels just right for a few pedal strokes around the block can end up feeling pretty wrong after 70 miles of roads. A good bike fit is essential for preventing most causes of knee pain.

For more guidance on what your knee pain means and strategies to avoid it, read on.

WANT MORE INFO ON BIKE FIT? CHECK OUT OUR EXCLUSIVE PROGRAM!

To help you figure out where to start, here are the most common types of cycling knee pain and the ways in which your bike fit may contribute to each symptom.

If your knee hurts right on the cap (or patella), it’s typically because of your quads. The four quadricep muscles attach to the shin via the patella, and when you’re putting force into your pedal stroke, these muscles deliver that force across the knee joint.

Your bike set-up can help with this problem. Determine whether adjusting your saddle height, saddle fore and aft, and/or crank length could alleviate the issue. Working with a professional bike fitter can be extremely helpful in addressing this type of knee pain.

“A saddle that is too low will keep your knee angle too tight at the top of the stroke, which increases the shear forces pulling the patella against the femur, which in turn increases the likelihood of tendonitis and harmful stresses in the cartilage behind the kneecap,” Veal says. “Likewise when the cranks are too long for your leg length, the knee joint is also too tight at the top of the stroke.”

How low is too low for a saddle? “For a quick reference to check if your saddle is the right height, have a seat and rest your heel on the pedal with the pedal in the 6 o’clock position,” says fit specialist and physical therapist Sara Bresnick, founder of Pedal Power Training Solutions in Medford, Massachusetts. “The knee of that leg should be straight. That equates to a 20- to 25-degree knee bend when clipped in.”

Riding with your saddle too far forward also can cause knee pain in the front, says Veal. “Your saddle should be positioned so the tibial tuberosity—or the bony bit below the kneecap—is directly above the ball of the foot, which in turn should be above the pedal spindle,” she says.

Also, be mindful of your form. Big-gear mashing, climbing in monster gears, and hard sprinting (especially if you’re not conditioned for it) can put undue stress on the knee and cause this type of pain.

If you do achieve a solid bike fit and avoid these common mistakes, and pain still persists, focus on stretching the quads to find relief.

Pain behind the knee is less common than pain in the front, and is generally easier to trace back to a culprit: over-extending the knee, says Bresnick. Your saddle is too high or too far back. “Try lowering the saddle a bit or moving it forward a bit in relation to the handlebars,” she says.

This pain is also more common among cyclists who spend a lot of time on fixed-gear bikes; When you ride fixed, you use your hamstrings to decelerate your pedal stroke, which can put the biceps femoris tendon (a hamstring muscle that runs down the back of your leg toward the outside of your knee) under too much load and irritate it. Giving your legs a break with some freewheeling now and then can also help.

If pain sticks around after making bike adjustments, try stretching the hamstrings regularly and avoid frequent out-of-saddle riding.

When you feel pain on the inner (or medial sides) of your knees, look down at your feet: Cleat placement is often a culprit, says Veal. Your cleat position affects your Q-factor, which dictates how far apart your feet are laterally when pedaling.

Ideally, the spacing should be that the loads from your knees to your pedals are traveling vertically without pushing the knee inward or outward, which stresses the ligaments on either side of your knee and can lead to pain.

Cleats positioned too close to the insides of your cycling shoes increase the distance between your feet, which can stress the inside collateral ligaments and cause pain in the inner (or medial) sides of your knees.

Too much float in your pedals also can cause medial knee pain. A little float—about 4.5 degrees—is all you need to be comfortable and keep your knees from getting stressed.

While a professional can help you adjust cleat positioning, you can also have someone take a slow-motion video you riding on a trainer, recording movement from the front of the bike. Look for asymmetry between your left and right side.

If you still feel pain on the inside of your knee after aligning your cleats, especially if it is a burning pain at rest or sharp pain when you start to walk or step up or down, you may have a type of bursitis. This pain typically improves with a warmup and stretching of the hip flexors and adductors (inner thighs).

Pain on the outer (or lateral) sides of the knees is often caused by iliotibial (IT) band syndrome—a stabbing pain that happens when the IT band (a fibrous connective tissue band that runs from the hip along the thigh to the tibia) becomes stressed and inflamed.

IT band issues can appear to come out of nowhere, and hurt most when the knee is at 20- to 30-degrees of flexion, like when you approach the 6 o’clock position and start to come back up.

“Misaligned cleats that cause the foot to be excessively toed in can cause this,” says Veal. So can cleats that are placed too far to the outsides of the shoes, causing too narrow of a stance on the bike.

If you think the cleats on your bike are misaligned, take your bike in for an adjustment. (A slow-mo video of you riding from the front can also help you see if your cleat positioning is to blame!)

Of course, what you do on your bike will also go a long way to promoting or alleviating knee pain. Here are some tips to assure it’s the latter.

Just as with most sports, a little warmup to get blood flowing and muscles primed is a good idea—so don’t skip it! As a general rule, aim for at least 15 minutes of moderate spinning before you attack the local climb or go hard on the flats.

Look at video of the pros in action, and you’ll notice their rapid and fluid pedal strokes. Try this drill to improve your pedal stroke: The next time you are going up your favorite climb, use a gear at least two teeth lower (thus easier) than usual. This higher cadence is easier on your joints. Think about making round circles as you pedal, not ovals.

Your first ride back after any extended amount of time off shouldn’t be five hours long. Instead, start with a lower mileage and build slowly.

Your body likes consistency, so when you alter equipment, your knees often protest. Whether you get a new bike, new shoes, new pedals, or change stem length, go easy at first to give yourself time to adapt.

Riding in 40-degree weather with red, chapped knees is a recipe for trouble. Pros routinely cover their legs in training when the temperature is below 60 degrees—that’s why knee warmers exist!

While each individual’s tolerance will differ, there’s certainly no harm in keeping muscles and joints warm. By using warmers, you can easily slip them off mid-ride if you start to warm up.

Take note of what gear works best in certain weather conditions, so you can repeat on future rides.

If knee pain persists, consider getting a professional bike fit. And no, we’re not talking about when a salesperson sets your seat height at purchase.

A professional bike fit should be an in-depth experience with a professionally trained fitter that includes an interview process, off-bike flexibility testing, and on-bike measurements and adjustments. Yes, it’s an investment (usually at least $200), but it’s worth it to ride pain-free. It could end up being the best money you ever spent on your cycling habit.

If you’re still experiencing cycling knee pain after doing everything mentioned above, including a professional bike fit, it may be caused by muscle imbalances instead—like weak glutes, hips, or core. It’s best to consult with a sports medicine physician and/or physical therapist to find the right course of treatment for you.

John Vasudevan, M.D. is an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania. He is board-certified in Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation and Sports Medicine. He is a Team Physician for UPenn Athletics and  medical director of the Broad Street Run and Philadelphia Distance Run, and previously for the Rock 'n' Roll Half-Marathon and Tri-Rock Triathlon in Philadelphia. He is a director of the running and endurance Sports Medicine Program at Penn Medicine.  Dr. Vasudevan provides non-operative management of musculoskeletal conditions affecting athletes and active individuals of all levels, and combines injury rehabilitation with injury prevention. He utilizes a variety of ultrasound-guided procedures and regenerative approaches such as platelet-rich plasma and percutaneous ultrasonic tenotomy. He sees patients at the Penn Medicine and the Philadelphia Veterans Administration hospital. Dr. Vasudevan attended medical school at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison. After his Transitional Year in Tucson, Arizona, he went to residency in PM&R at Thomas Jefferson University in Philadelphia and onwards to Stanford University for his fellowship in Sports Medicine. He has been in practice at the University of Pennsylvania since 2012.

#8869. ‘Relishing the Moment’: A Runner Ran 2:49 at the NYC Marathon—Dressed as a Hot Dog

Sarah Pezzino nearly gave up on running. Soon, she could own a Guinness World Record.

I ran Sunday's New York City Marathon in some of my finest FlipBelt gear and spent the final five miles dealing with cramps, a full stomach, and legs that were mad at me for taking on this course willingly for the third time. As for Sarah Pezzino, her race went a little differently.

The 23-year-old from Easton, Pennsylvania, showed up to the starting line in Staten Island dressed as a hot dog and finished in 2:49:15, which, after hearing, made me think I could’ve done a lot more than just iron my name onto my tank top.

Pezzino, a personal trainer and group fitness coach, was attempting to break a Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon dressed as a savory food. The previous mark was 3:11:34, which, incredibly, she beat by more than 22 minutes! Guinness still has to review the evidence before anything becomes official, but judging by the number of people who noticed her on Sunday, finding witnesses won't be a problem.

When speaking with Runner’s World, Pezzino said the hot dog wasn't even originally part of her marathon plans—and neither, for a while, was running another marathon at all.

Pezzino had been competing since childhood, starting in a local running series at age 4 before moving on to cross country and track in high school and college. She made her marathon debut in Chicago in 2024. She returned the following year, but a serious medical emergency at Mile 17 forced her to drop out. Afterward, she strongly considered giving up running altogether.

"I'd put too much pressure on myself and lost the joy in the sport," she told Runner's World.

A close friend helped convince her to give racing another chance, and they came up with a plan to run Chicago and New York in 2026, raise money for the Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation (MMRF), and get their friends and community involved along the way. With any luck, doing this would be a chance to enjoy running again without making every race about the clock.

Pezzino had a deep personal connection to the fundraising part of their plans. She lost her mother to a rare cancer in 2022, and Mike, the husband of a close family friend, died from multiple myeloma. She had partnered with MMRF for her first marathon and wanted to reconnect with the organization. With help from her coworkers at CycleFit Lehigh Valley, she organized everything from raffles and 6Ks to ice cream scooping and what they called “no-shower happy hours.” All these fundraising efforts brought in more than $8,000.

And sometime during all that planning, someone suggested she run New York as a hot dog.

A friend had spotted a costume at Target, so Pezzino went to see it for herself. She tried it on, filmed a video of herself running through the aisles, and sent it to the group. "The next thing I knew, I was walking out of Target with a hot dog costume," she recalled.

The Guinness idea came later, when she started looking into potential records and discovered the savory food category. By September, she'd committed to the attempt, despite the rather obvious logistical challenge of actually running 26.2 miles in the thing, which was labeled as suitable for ages 8 and up.

That left a lot of leeway. Pezzino said the body fit an adult, but the headpiece was considerably smaller, so she wore it as a hood instead. Someone from CycleFit helped tailor the sides, which helped.

Her total mileage running in the outfit before race day? Three miles, completed the day before.

Fortunately, New York's cool weather on race day worked in her favor, and she didn't experience the overheating or chafing that could've made for a miserable afternoon. She carried a Nathan handheld water bottle through the first 20 miles to help with fueling, and the costume itself gave her surprisingly little trouble.

"The biggest issue was getting it off afterward, when it was all sweaty," she said.

Race morning brought plenty of attention, even before she'd crossed the starting line. Runners asked whether she intended to wear the costume the entire way or ditch it with her throwaway clothes. Pezzino happily posed for pictures, and once she got moving, the commentary from spectators was about what you'd expect.

She heard plenty of "HOOOT DOOOG!" along the course, plus more than a few people yelling, "Look at that glizzy!"

Pezzino was enjoying herself enough that she barely thought about the record. Three weeks earlier, she'd run a personal best 2:45:57 in Chicago, but New York was an entirely different experience, with no thought to chasing another PR, even with the Guinness attempt on the line.

"In New York, my mind was nowhere near the clock," she said. "It was set on having fun, embracing the crowds, seeing the city, and taking the race mile by mile."

She spent much of the race chatting with other runners, jumping into photos, and enjoying the crowds rather than sweating her splits. And when she reached Central Park, she found herself celebrating a finish that would have seemed pretty unlikely a year earlier.

She'd even attracted some attention from a familiar and very famous face, who was serving as grand marshal for the event.

"Tracy Morgan saw me finish and said, 'I hope that hot dog is relishing this moment,'" Pezzino recalled.

Within seconds, Pezzino said, a broadcaster had pulled her aside for an interview and clipped a microphone onto the mustard portion of her costume. She was still trying to wrap her head around what she'd accomplished, which seems fair considering she'd just run a sub-three-hour marathon dressed as something you'd order at a baseball game.

Of everything that happened on Sunday, though, Pezzino's favorite moment came just before the finish, when she spotted her friends and CycleFit teammates cheering in the final 200 meters. These were the people who'd encouraged her to return to racing, helped with the fundraising, and supported her through two marathons in three weeks. Having them there as she finished meant more to her than any reaction to the costume.

"I didn't cross a single finish line this year alone," she said.

#8868. The Cervélo Soloist—The Race-Inspired Road Bike That Makes Sense for the Way Most Riders Actually Ride

A race-inspired road bike built for riders who want one fast machine for climbs, descents, and pacelines.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Over the last few years, many bike brands have tried to combine the benefits of their aero bike platform and climbing bikes into an all-arounder. When I managed a Trek store, the brand launched the Madone Gen8. Trek intended it as the next logical step in its road bike lineup by combining the Madone’s speed with the Émonda’s low weight. Other examples of this trend include the Specialized Tarmac and Cannondale’s SuperSix Evo.

Cervélo touts the Soloist as its do-everything road platform. While you’ll see its S5 and R5 at races like the Tour de France, the Soloist probably won’t show up at the starting line of any Grand Tours. That’s because the Cervélo-sponsored Visma-Lease a Bike team doesn’t need a third road bike; it already has race-winning aero bikes and dedicated climbing bikes for its athletes. Most days those riders use the S5, and on the steepest alpine climbs they can go with the R5.

But most of us don’t have the money, space, or desire to own multiple road bikes to choose between depending on the route we’re riding that day. One road bike that flies up climbs, inspires confidence on descents, and holds well in a paceline is the key for many riders. After almost three months of riding, I found Cervélo’s Soloist fits right into that sweet spot.

The Soloist mixes the pure speed of the S5 with the uphill float of the R5. It sits between both models in weight—about a pound heavier than the R5 and about two pounds lighter than the S5. Visually, the Soloist looks like a midpoint between both bikes. It brings the lines of the R5 while tying in the aero aesthetics of the S5, but the geometry charts paint a different picture. The Soloist leans toward the S5 when looking at the geometry charts for each model. When shopping the Cervélo lineup consider the pricing. The Ultegra Di2 model of the S5 and R5 are both listed at $10,100. The Soloist gives the benefits of each bike, and saves you almost $2,000 for the Ultegra Di2 model.

The Soloist lineup ranges from $6,800 for the SRAM Rival AXS model up to $11,000 for the SRAM Red AXS–equipped bike. I tested the Shimano Ultegra Di2-equipped version, which sells for $8,250. This bike comes stock with a 4iii power meter, an integrated carbon bar and stem, and carbon wheels. My 54cm test bike weighed 15.9 pounds without the bottles or the pedals—pretty respectable for an aero-ish bike with Ultegra components.

Straight out of the box, it was almost ready to roll. Although Cervélo equips this bike with many parts I’d choose for my own bike, I swapped out the stock 700x29c Vittoria Corsa Next TLR G2.0 tires after only a few rides. The rubber was okay on flatter rides, but lacked the grip and ride feel I wanted on twisting descents.

Installing 28mm Pirelli P Zero TLR Race tires was exactly what the Soloist needed to elevate my confidence on descents. The tires made the bike feel locked-in when leaning into turns (I even bagged a couple of Strava trophies on our local descents).

The Soloist ships with aero bottles. Cervélo claims the bottles save 4.3 watts compared to standard round bottles. However, that savings doesn’t matter if you’re wasting energy fumbling with your bottles. The aero ones fit so tight in their cages I almost fell on my first ride trying to remove one.

Even after weeks of testing, I didn’t get used to these bidons. I’ve tried other aero bottle setups and haven’t had the same issue. Plus, the stock aero cages that come with the bike don’t pair as well with traditional round bottles as some brands’ aero cages.

For my first ride, I dove right into the deep end by taking the Soloist up Fiddler’s Elbow. This notorious mile-and-a-half climb gains a little over 700 feet with grades that exceed 20 percent near its summit.

I’ve done this climb at least twenty times on my Trek Madone, with gearing that is a bit more favorable for climbing than the Soloist’s 36x34t lowest gear. But even with taller gearing, the Cervélo floated up the climb. The bike’s geometry put me in a comfortable position, and I appreciated the Soloist’s lower weight on steeper parts of the climb.

But the Soloist didn’t only excel on climbs. The backside of Fiddler’s features a twisting, high-speed descent where maintaining your line is critical, and the bike felt stable. Once I reached the bottom, I had rolling farm roads back to the office, similar to where I did the bulk of my daily rides with this bike.

The Soloist shines on undulating rural roads and group rides. Sometimes our office lunch rides lean toward a spicier pace, with a single or double paceline of up to eight riders. The Soloist is calm, collected, and easy to ride in groups, and its aerodynamics helped when I started to fall off the back and had to catch back to the group.

Lastly, since you don’t always ride on butter-smooth tarmac, I also tested the Soloist on roads outside of its typical scope. The bike felt confident, even on some of the chunky gravel roads. However, I don’t recommend doing this too often with the Soloist; it doesn’t have enough tire clearance for actual gravel tread.

The bike proved easy to ride and live with. I wish I didn’t have to send the Soloist back to Cervélo, as I’d gladly spend more hours on this bike.

Bicycling’s Test Editor, Dan Chabanov, felt like the previous model tried to mix the benefits of the R5 and S5, but missed the mark. “I found it pretty unremarkable. Not in a bad way, but compared to other bikes at the time it just kind of split everything down the middle. It wasn’t very aero but it was aero-ish. It wasn’t very light, but it wasn’t overly heavy. It did a lot of stuff well, but it never really wowed me,” says Chabanov.

The new model irons out those wrinkles. Cervélo shaved nearly a pound off the Ultegra model and added more aero features from the S5—notably the integrated handlebar and stem combination.

I’m impressed after a few months using the new-generation Soloist as my primary road bike. It climbs better than other comparable bikes I’ve tried, holds a pocket in a paceline well, and descends like a banshee. Many brands have tried to blend the watt savings of an aero bike and the weight of a climbing bike. Cervélo took a swing with the previous Soloist model, but refined the previous generation to create a well-blended machine.

This bike is the great choice for everyone from the local crit ripper to the Saturday coffee shop ride champion. If you get this bike, then pick up a pair of Pirelli P Zero Race tires or Continental GP 5000 tires to unlock its full potential. This bike is at the top of my list for those of us who want to have one road bike at home that can rip every ride.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8866. Trek’s New Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

After riding the $11,499 SLR, I think the $4,200 SL 6 AXS is the smartest buy.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

This Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here. Next, I want to hear what you think. Bicycling members can continue the discussion with me on Discord, where I’ll answer questions and hear how the Domane works for riders beyond my test. The invitation appears after the review.

If you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the new Domane belongs on your list. It feels more eager under power than previous versions, while keeping the stability and confidence that have always made the bike good at everyday riding.

The version I’d point most people toward is the $4,200 SL 6 AXS. It gets the same geometry, tire clearance, and basic frame features as the expensive SLR models, along with electronic shifting and carbon wheels. The SLR saves weight and opens the door to Trek’s Project One customization. Those are real advantages, but they don’t make it a fundamentally different bike.

I tested the $11,499 SLR 9 AXS 2x. It weighed 16.3 pounds in size M. The bike I’d recommend first costs less than half as much.

BIKE TESTED: Trek Gen. 5 Domane SLR 9 AXS 2xACTUAL WEIGHT 16.3 pounds (Size M, as tested) USE Road, light gravel PRICE AS TESTED $11,499 MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,400 to $11,499; $14,999 limited edition ICON No. 76FRAME ONLY OPTION: Yes. $3,700 (SLR) $2,000 (SL)CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS Yes, SLR models through Project One SIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, ML, L, XL WEIGHT LIMIT 125 kg/275 lb (bicycle, rider, and cargo) TIRE CLEARANCE 40mm BB STANDARD T47 threaded BRAKE HOSE ROUTING Internal, RCS headset; under bar/stem on most buildsDRIVETRAIN COMPATIBILITY 1x and 2x, electronic shifting only DERAILLEUR HANGER UDH WARRANTY Lifetime, frame and rigid fork, original owner CRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, Trek Carbon Care discounted replacement

I’ve ridden every generation of the Domane, including several of the more aggressive RSL versions. Over the years, Trek added adjustable IsoSpeed, front IsoSpeed, internal storage, aero shaping, and hidden cables. The fifth-generation bike pulls back on much of that.

The Gen 5 feels more solid and reactive underfoot than its predecessors. It’s stiffer when I get on the pedals, accelerates with more snap, and climbs with a crispness that used to elude the Domane. In that way, it feels more like a Madone than any previous version.

It hasn’t lost the stability and confidence that make the Domane a good everyday road bike. I can push it hard down a descent without feeling like I’m taking a test of nerves. The fit is excellent, too. The taller front end should help more riders find a position that’s comfortable and aerodynamic.

And no, it doesn’t feel slow on 35mm tires. The bike feels quick and responsive. The wider tires are part of what makes it work, not an anchor holding it back.

The original Domane’s signature feature was IsoSpeed, a mechanism that let the seat tube flex to add comfort. Trek developed it over several generations, then removed it from the bike that introduced it.

The new Domane gets much of its comfort from wider tires at lower pressures, along with frame and seatpost tuning. Most models come with 35mm tires, and the frame clears up to 40mm. Trek says that combination provides enough comfort that IsoSpeed’s remaining benefit isn’t worth its weight and complexity.

IsoSpeed still works. Trek told me that with the same 35mm tires, the Gen 4 transmits slightly less vibrational energy than the Gen 5. Trek also says the Gen 5 on 35mm tires comes within 5 percent of the Gen 4 on its stock 32mm tires at the rear. At the front, Trek says the two generations perform similarly.

Those are Trek’s test results, not measurements I made. But the decision makes sense to me. Wider tires add traction and capability that IsoSpeed couldn’t provide. Trek decided the system’s remaining comfort advantage wasn’t enough to justify keeping it.

If you own an older Domane, what did IsoSpeed do for you? Did you notice a difference when you moved to wider tires, or do you miss the old system? I’d like to hear what you’ve felt on real roads.

According to Trek’s white paper, the Gen 5 frame is about 292 grams lighter than Gen 4. It also eliminates IsoSpeed and its associated maintenance.

The frame uses a threaded T47 bottom bracket, a round fork steerer, a Universal Derailleur Hanger, and a standard 27.2mm seatpost. For a modern performance bike, there’s not much proprietary weirdness here. That’s a feature.

The internal storage compartment is gone, too. I’ll miss it. It was useful. Trek says its research showed that many Domane owners weren’t using it. The new frame retains fender mounts, top-tube mounts, and frame-bag mounts. I like the trade: less hardware and complexity, with straightforward ways to carry gear when you need to.

The cable routing is another smart compromise. On most models, brake hoses run beneath the two-piece bar and stem before entering the frame at the headset. It looks clean, but changing a bar or stem doesn’t become a major repair job. Fit changes and service matter more to me than hiding every cable at any cost.

The SL and SLR share the same geometry, tire clearance, seatpost size, bottom bracket, UDH, and general feature set. The SL uses Trek’s 500 Series carbon; the SLR uses lighter 900 Series carbon. Trek says both frames are designed to the same stiffness requirements. The SL supports mechanical drivetrains; the SLR is electronic-shifting only.

The SLR primarily buys lower weight, access to Trek’s highest-end builds, and the ability to customize components through Project One. Buyers can specify details such as crank length, handlebar width, and stem length. If you’re spending this much on a bike, getting those dimensions right from the factory is a meaningful advantage.

But the SLR doesn’t change the core experience enough to be the obvious choice for most riders. I’d look closely at the $4,200 SL 6 AXS first. It has a carbon frame, electronic shifting, carbon wheels, 40mm tire clearance, and the same accessible fit. The carbon range starts at $2,400 with the Tiagra SL 4. The SLR 9 AXS 2x I tested costs $11,499.

Trek also offers an ultralight SLR 9 AXS 1x with 28mm tires. Trek describes it as the racier interpretation of the Domane, but it did not vibration-test that configuration. If comfort is a big reason you’re considering the bike, pay attention to the tire setup, not just the frame name.

If you’re shopping for a Domane, which versions are you weighing? Would you spend more for the SLR’s lower weight and Project One options, or put that money toward another bike or gear?

Trek says it applied aero lessons from the Gen 8 Madone, but aerodynamics weren’t a major priority. In a pedaling-mannequin test, Trek claims the Gen 5 improved by 0.6 watts over Gen 4.

That seems appropriate. Trek prioritized weight, simplicity, and ride quality instead of chasing another aero headline.

The fifth-generation Domane is an excellent road bike. It’s light, comfortable, stable, and lively. It’s easier to adjust and service than many integrated performance bikes, retains useful mounts, and drops features that added weight and complexity without improving the bike enough to justify them.

The old Domanes were more technically adventurous. I miss that part of the story more than I miss riding them.

For most riders, I think Gen 5 is the right Trek road bike. The SL 6 AXS is the model I’d point people toward first. The SLR makes sense if you want the lighter frame and factory customization, but the expensive build doesn’t change the core experience. Taken as a whole, the new Domane is my favorite drop-bar bike Trek makes.

That’s my take after riding the bike. Now I want to hear from people who own a Domane, have ridden an earlier version, or are considering the Gen 5. What questions do you still have? What would you like me to investigate or compare? I’ll continue the conversation on Discord and bring the most useful questions and experiences back here.

What do you think of the new Trek Domane? What questions do you still have? What did I screw up? If you own or have ridden the Gen 5 Domane, share your impressions.

Bicycling members can join me in The Test Ride on Discord to continue this review. The invitation is below.

Find the Trek Gen 5 Domane post in the bike-reviews forum. Tell me what you ride and what you’re deciding between. Your feedback and insights will help me write better reviews.

#8865. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Half Marathon

Run your first or fastest half marathon with the support of walk intervals.

Runners can’t get enough of the half marathon—and for good reason. Not only is it a practical and challenging distance for all levels of runners, but it’s also a race widely offered at running events across the country. Dig through race calendars, and you’ll likely find plenty of half marathons in bucket-list locations and even your own backyard.

And whether you’re looking to run your first or best half marathon, the run/walk method could be the smart, sustainable strategy you need to strongly cross the finish line.

Runner’s World’s program, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, give you the training tools and plans necessary to conquer the 13.1-mile distance with walk intervals. Beginners and experienced run/walkers can find one of several training plans that fit their goals and give them confidence in their physical and mental fitness heading into race day.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Half Marathon, we’ll teach you:

The half marathon consistently ranks as one of the most popular race distances among runners. According to the 2026 RunningUSA Global Runner Survey, 38 percent of nearly 12,000 surveyed runners said the half was their favorite event—20 percentage points higher than the next most preferred distance (the marathon). The run/walk method can make the distance manageable for all levels of runners and even help you get a new personal record.

“I ran my best half marathon using run/walk during the Savannah Rock ’n’ Roll Half Marathon,” says run/walker Cheryl Munn. “It was really hot. People were dropping like flies. I was able to maintain and be consistent by just keeping up the intervals.”

To find your goal half marathon pace, use your data from your Magic Mile time trial. Multiply your timed mile by 1.2 to get your half marathon race pace. You’ll also use that pace to set your training paces and run/walk intervals you’ll use during your buildup to race day.

Runner’s World has three run/walk training plans to choose from to prepare for your half marathon: a beginner, intermediate, and advanced plan. Over anywhere from six to 16 weeks, you’ll incorporate run/walk workouts, easy walks, long runs, cross-training sessions, and rest days into your training block to build your endurance, speed, and confidence ahead of your half marathon.

Ideal for: Runners who have never completed a half marathon before.

Using this plan, you’ll have two midweek run/walk workouts lasting 30 to 45 minutes each week, along with one easy walk for 20 to 45 minutes, two days with a cross-training option, and at least one rest day. You’ll also have weekend long runs, which start at two miles and work up to 14 miles—longer than the 13.1-mile race distance. Pushing just past the half marathon mark in training will help you build endurance and prepare your body for the

Pro tip: If you’re new to the run/walk method, start your workouts with five to 10 seconds of running, and then walk the rest of the minute. Or, if you’ve been using run/walk for at least three months, you can follow our run/walk ratio suggestion chart to determine your ideal ratio.

Ideal for: Athletes who have been running at least three times a week for three to six months and want to work up from a 5K to a half marathon.

Each week with this plan, you’ll complete two midweek run/walk workouts lasting 30 to 45 minutes, an easy walk, two optional cross-training days, and one rest day. You’ll start with five miles for your first long run and progress to 14 miles by week six. Compared to the beginner plan, the intermediate plan features an increase in mileage.

Ideal for: Runners who have already raced a half marathon before and want to improve their time. You’ll also want to have a solid fitness base before starting the plan, making sure you can complete double-digit miles.

This plan features speedwork once a week, as well as race pace miles one to two times per week based on your Magic Mile time trial. You’ll also have two optional cross-training days and a rest day each week. Your long run begins at five miles and progresses to 14 to 17 miles toward the end of the training block.

A staple speed workout you complete following the advanced plan is 800-meter repeats. You’ll run at 30 seconds per mile faster than your half race pace for 800 meters, followed by 400 meters of walking—which you’ll repeat until you hit your target amount of reps. For example, if your half marathon pace is 12 minutes per mile, you’ll run at 11:30 pace for 800 meters for each rep. For your half marathon pace work, you’ll incorporate race pace miles into both your midweek and long run mileage, allowing you to practice your goal speed and run/walk interval ratios.

Remember all of that patient, consistent work you put in during training? Trust that preparation on race day. It’s tempting to get caught up in the race day atmosphere and complete your first adrenaline-filled miles way too fast. As you begin your race, keep your run/walk ratio and goal pace in mind, and pace yourself strategically in the early miles so you don’t burn out.

The half marathon is such a popular distance that the race course may be flooded with other athletes. As a run/walk athlete, keep in mind that not every runner around you will be taking walk breaks or taking them at the same time as you. #8864. Anita Herbert Shares Her Upper-Body Smith Machine Workout

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

There’s nothing quite like lifting a barbell loaded with weighted plates when you are looking to dial in your resistance training efforts, but for many people, the idea of balancing a free weight seems daunting, and for others, mobility issues or a lack of experience can become a serious obstacle. It’s good to know then, that buff beauty Anita Herbert has sculpted herself into phenomenal shape by including the Smith machine into her rotation.

“Here are some of my favorite back and shoulder exercises you can add to your next upper body session, using just a Smith machine,” offered the Hungarian in a recent Instagram post for her “Fit Queen Army” on Instagram. This fit female is not only a transformative coach, but she is also an IFBB Pro. “Save this for your next upper body day!” Herbert advised her 150,000-plus followers.

The “FitQueen” showed how to get the most from each machine

Machines, just like free weights, can build muscle by progressive overload, and this session is stacked with plenty of heavy reps. Aim for 8 to 12 on each exercise to put your body into a state of hypertrophy, forcing to adaptations that will build your muscles back stronger.

For her first superset, the Fit Queen begins with the shoulder press, primarily working her anterior deltoid at the front of the shoulder, and also recruiting the upper back, triceps, and core. Next, using a supinated grip, comes the inverted row for taxing the mid-back, lats, and rear delts.

The second superset calls for a pullup that is great for athletes of any level, because you will raise your body from a seated position, and can use the feet for further stabilization. Using a wide grip, pause for a short time at the top of the lift, in order to increase time under tension. This will work the lats, rhomboids, and upper trapezius, but be sure not to shrug, and concentrate on a smooth range of motion. This exercise is followed by the single arm shoulder press, to fix any strength imbalances and fire up those front deltoids once again.

The third and final superset starts with a single-arm row, hitting the lats, traps, and rear delts, while also activating the rotator cuff and forearms. Keep your core braced and focus on engaging the back, while keeping the elbows close to the body. The last move is the upright row for building some serious boulder shoulders. You will also work the triceps and upper back as you improve grip strength all at the same time.

While it is true that the Smith machine stabilizes the weight and reduces the chance of injury, you may be surprised to find that the load can feel heavier on this device.

“It can feel heavier than free weights, especially for upper body exercises because Smith machines have different bar weights, counterbalance systems and resistance,” explained Herbert, who provided further advice to her seriously impressed followers in the comments section. “The fixed bar path also changed how the movement feels, compared to free weights.”

#8863. No Alps, No Pyrenees, and No Paris. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes Will Still Deliver Exciting Racing, but the Women Deserve More of Cycling’s Iconic Backdrops.

A three-day start in England and a finish atop the Puy de Dôme give us plenty to look forward to. But some of the organizers’ choices leave me wondering what this Tour could have been.

The route of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift was revealed in late October, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a jaunt through central France, and a summit finish atop the Puy de Dôme. The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour will kick off on Friday, July 30, and conclude on Saturday, August 7, after nine days of racing.

In just five editions, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift has become the pinnacle of the women’s WorldTour calendar. And looking at the 2027 route, we’re in for another nine days of aggressive racing, a hard-fought GC battle, and opportunities for a wide range of stage winners. Yet some route choices leave me lukewarm, and a few things are missing altogether. There’s no trek into the Alps or Pyrenees, no individual time trial, and still no Paris finale.

Now, I don’t doubt that the women’s peloton will make the most of the route it’s given, but whether it’ll match the spectacle of previous editions is another question.

First, the highlights, starting with the three-day Grand Départ in England.

The 2027 route puts a lot of the fireworks up front, so there’s no easing into this Tour. It opens with a short, punchy 86km stage from Leeds to Manchester. Officially classified as flat, it still packs in three categorized climbs. So while the sprinters may get their chance at the first yellow jersey, it’s not guaranteed. Then comes a bumpy stage two that, a local tells me, is much harder on the legs than it looks on paper. And then we’ll get the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift’s first team time trial in London.

Leeds, Manchester, London. The 2027 edition will put women’s racing in front of millions. That’s a huge opportunity to draw roadside crowds and reach new audiences. Those opening stages could also give the GC an intriguing shape. An early winner backed by a strong team performance in London might carry a rider in yellow deep into the race.

Then there’s the Puy de Dôme. The volcano occupies a special place in cycling history, having hosted 14 men’s Tour de France stage finishes, including the famous 1964 head-to-head between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor.

A more recent memory of the Puy de Dôme is that of Matteo Jorgenson’s heartbreak on stage nine of the 2023 Tour. The American attacked alone with almost 50km remaining, only for Canadian Michael Woods to catch and pass him some 450 meters from victory. Jorgenson ultimately finished fourth.

It’s easy to imagine the volcano hosting another exciting chapter in the Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon//SRAM) and Demi Vollering (FDJ United–Suez) rivalry.

In 2025, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift delivered six different stage winners and three riders in yellow. This year, it was six and five respectively. The 2027 route should again give a broad cast of riders their chance, with plenty of terrain for versatile stage hunters alongside opportunities for the sprinters and climbers.

That’s something I like about the Tour. A Tour stage can define a rider’s season; just look at the breakthrough victories of Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L'Imad), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education–Oatly), and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance–Soudal) in years past.

The route opens the door to well-rounded riders, but the overall will still likely be decided on the final two mountainous days. But if climbing decides the Tour, I’d like to see some high-mountain racing in the Alps or Pyrenees. If the intention is to give more riders a shot at the GC, then I want to believe that they can actually take the yellow home, rather than just borrow it for a few days.

Of course, Vollering and Niewiadoma excel on punchy terrain too. And that’s part of my concern: different profiles don’t guarantee different outcomes. Perhaps the shorter climbs will keep more riders in contention, but I’m not convinced this route broadens the fight for yellow as much as it prolongs it.

Then there’s London. I’m excited about the setting, but the racing format leaves me underwhelmed. I prefer an individual time trial where every rider controls her own performance. No matter the timing rules, a team time trial tends to favor stronger, bigger teams, with more money to spend on a deeper roster, equipment, testing, and optimizing. A rider from a team with fewer resources could leave London with a time loss that reflects her team's budget more than her own performance.

Eighteen kilometers may limit the damage, but as 2024 showed, when Niewiadoma-Phinney won the overall by just four seconds, every single second counts.

While Britain gets the big-city showcases, I feel roadside fans in France get a bad deal. The route bypasses the country’s largest cities on its way to a finale where spectator access remains uncertain.

Strict environmental protections are in place on Puy de Dôme, and organizers are still exploring if they can admit a limited crowd at the summit. I understand the need for protection, but a repeat of 2023’s empty upper slopes would be a lonely way to welcome in the Tour winner. If fans aren’t welcome, surely it’s worth asking whether this is the right place to finish.

And while a summit finish can deliver exciting racing, I’m still waiting to see the women’s peloton finish on the cobblestones of Paris, same as the men. Wout van Aert’s victory in 2025 and Mathieu van der Poel’s all-out effort in 2026 were absolute highlights of those Tours for me. The Montmartre circuit has shown how much racing in Paris can offer, beyond a ceremonial procession. After watching Vollering and Niewiadoma duel in France and again in Montréal, with Marlen Reusser never far behind, I want to see what these women could do on those streets.

#8862. The 6 Best Walking Pads for Staying Active During the Workday

Improve your focus and get your steps in seamlessly with one of these walking pads.

Stuck at your desk all day? Us, too—and we work for a running publication. (Oh, the irony!) Well, fret not, fellow office warriors: Walking pads and under-desk treadmills are here to save the day—and boost your step count. These low-profile treadmills slide right under your standing desk, making it easy to walk and work at the same time. Thanks to a renewed focus on health, whether you’re working from home or heading into the office, walking pads have quickly become a staple in home offices and shared workspaces alike. So, whether you’re aiming to close those rings or boost your daily steps, a walking pad can help you stay active throughout the workday without missing that 3 p.m. meeting.

Recent studies support the benefits of movement while working: office employees using treadmill desks have reported improved energy, greater focus, and a boosted mood over just a few months of consistent use. Plus, the convenience of walking pads means you can exercise regardless of the weather or your schedule—no gym membership required. With so many walking pads on the market, each offering a unique blend of features and portability, at a range of prices, finding the right model can be overwhelming. Not to worry, though. We put tens of thousands of steps on these machines to find the best ones for you.

If you’re looking for portability, a cushioned deck, affordability, and a walking pad you can use while you’re in the office without people on your meeting hearing your treadmill? This is the one for you. We’ve had it at HQ for years, and it’s consistently in use by our team. It has seen thousands of miles, and it’s still going.

It’s got a well-cushioned deck that absorbs impact, a motor built for heavier walkers, and it’s relatively wide for a walking pad. It is, however, a bit short front-to-back, but it’s fine for most people. If you’re a giant like my brother? You might want a different model, otherwise, this is just about perfect.

If your social feeds are overflowing with DeerRun under-desk walking pads, you’re not alone. This TikTok-famous gadget is everywhere, and for good reason: It’s a simple, space-saving treadmill that you can control with a remote or an app.

The app’s got your back, letting you dial up the speed without breaking a sweat (or your focus). And topping out at just over 3 mph, it’s more of a gentle stroll than a full-on sprint.

The deck’s a cozy—if kinda tight—35 by 16 inches, which means it’ll tuck neatly under your desk. It’s easy to use and that glorious cushioned feel is pure bliss for your feet while you’re getting those steps in.

This is our office’s new BFF. The most frequent user, Hype Director Aly Ellis, said that her favorite feature is the convenience, noting “I prefer this one to one with arms because it allows me to adjust the desk height when I need to for comfort purposes.” She’s also a big fan of the fact that it lights up, but mostly because it’s cool. I agree. She does worry about losing the remote, as we all do, but fun fact! You can operate it via the app, so there’s no real worry there.

It’s quiet and sturdy, has a 12 percent incline, and has a high weight limit, so larger-bodied walkers should feel comfortable on this walking pad.

This is easily the most compact on this list. It folds up to about the size of a queen blanket, but it doesn’t feel flimsy or cheap. WalkingPad has made it its business to build high-quality walking pads that are made for your home or office.

I like this one because it’s no fuss, no muss, has a large 48-inch by 16-inch walking surface, weighs only 50 pounds, and it’s whisper quiet.

The Urevo Strol 2.0 walking pad is the under-desk treadmill you want if you tend toward boredom. It has a ton of built-in programming, and the ability to connect to a ton more like Zwift.

Once you link the app to your phone, you can control everything right there. But, if that’s not your style, traditional controls are easy to access and use. It’s a smooth walk, quieter than previous models, and you can move it around easily.

The combination of the sturdy tablet holder and smart app integration creates a user-friendly experience that blends exercise with productivity or entertainment effortlessly in any space.

If you’ve ever wondered how hard you can push yourself while you work, do I have the walking pad for you. This puppy inclines all the way to 14 percent, which—whoa—and it does it with the power of a brushless motor, which makes it quieter (though it can’t quiet your huffing and puffing), and that same motor will last a lot longer than others thanks to its construction.

The whole thing is remote controlled, so when you’re fighting for your life and you don’t want your Teams meeting to see it, you can quickly adjust on the fly.

When shopping for the best under-desk walking pad, keep these factors in mind:

Size and Portability: Ensure the walking pad’s dimensions fit under your desk and in your workspace. Consider weight and whether the machine has wheels for easy storage or movement.

Belt Size: Wider belts provide more stability and comfort, while narrower pads are better for tight spaces. Longer deck lengths work best for those with a longer stride.

Speed Range: Most walking pads offer speeds from 0.5 to 4 mph—enough for gentle walking to brisk paces. Some 2-in-1 pads allow faster speeds when used away from a desk.

Incline Options: A few models feature adjustable inclines for varied intensity, though many are flat for multitasking. If you want more of a workout, look for pads with at least a minor incline capability.

Weight Capacity: Check each machine’s weight limit, especially if you need extra support or want a more robust frame.

Noise Level: Choose a quiet pad for minimal distraction, particularly if you share your space with others or take calls frequently.

Ease of Use: Look for simple controls (often via remote) and clear displays. Consider features like app compatibility, folding capabilities, and maintenance requirements.

Price: Budget models are available for under $200, while high-end or commercial-grade options cost significantly more. Decide which features are worth extra investment for your specific needs.

So, what’s the difference between a treadmill and a walking pad? There are a lot of parallels for sure, and functionally they’re very similar. However, the real difference between a treadmill and a walking pad happens under the hood. Walking pads have smaller, quieter motors that don’t allow you to pick up the pace dramatically, but they keep them quiet enough to use while you work or read. They’re also a lot lower to the ground, and that low step height makes them a great choice for folks who have joint and mobility issues. They’re shorter and narrower than traditional treadmills so that they fit easily under desks. Luckily, they’re also easier to store, and many of them fold into little packages or can be stored on their side. And the point many people love the most? They’re usually a lot cheaper.

Our team performed all walking pad testing either in our offices for hundreds of hours or in our own homes, reflecting the real-world environments where these products are most used. Each unit was assessed with a focus on:

Speed and Incline: We measured each pad’s speed range and, where available, incline adjustments, making sure transitions were smooth and controls responsive.

Noise: We operated pads during conference calls and regular work to evaluate how quietly each model ran.

Design and Portability: We checked for ease of setup, the ability to move and store the pad, and whether the design fit under multiple desk types.

User Experience: Testers of varying heights and stride lengths used each pad for sessions extending beyond an hour, noting comfort, usability, and any unique features or challenges.

Every product featured here was rigorously tested for durability, performance, and portability in the Runner’s World offices and in the homes of our editors, ensuring our recommendations are both practical and trustworthy. Whether you’re a remote worker, student, or just trying to reduce your sedentary hours, our comprehensive guide will help you find the best under-desk walking pad to fit your space and support your movement goals.

Model and actor Chase Mattson has become one of vertical media’s most sought after actors, so when the star was asked to chop it up with the superstars of WWE for ReelShort’s Agent of Shadows, he went all-in, gaining respect for these larger-than-life talents in the process, and telling M&F that he prepares himself for any challenge through serious training and a dedicated attitude to nutrition.

In today’s world, vertical media makes sense. As younger people shun the traditional television and scroll away on social media, the premise of shooting shows vertically allows for seamless viewing on phones. Still, with vertical micro-dramas offering free episodes before a pay wall hides the ending, the pressure to perform to the best of his abilities, for every second, is not lost on Chase Mattson, who was recently named People magazine’s Sexiest ReelShort Star. He’s also become one of the genre’s most able actors.

Mattson’s latest project is titled Agent of Shadows, and is a collaboration between ReelShort and WWE, featuring grapplers such as Drew McIntyre, Booker T, Jacob Fatu, and Nikkita Lyons. And, while Mattson, himself was a highly active athlete in his youth, the 6’3” star was in awe of the likes of McIntyre, who is 6’5.” “I was told that Drew was a big guy and I was like, ‘okay cool, I’m a big guy,’ and then he came on set and this dude is a giant, man!” Fortunately, the star says that he and McIntyre became fast friends.”

Among Mattson’s preferred workouts is the “Cindy” workout, a CrossFit circuit that  Tom Holland has employed to stay in Spider-Man shape. To try it, you’ll perform 5 pullups, 10 pushups, and 15 air squats, then repeat for as many rounds as you can. “I was like, that seems too easy but the first time, I got to round eight, and I was gassed,” shares Mattson. Now, the actor has reached a peak of 16 rounds and is even pushing himself further by squatting with 40-pound dumbbells.

With four kids (and two dogs), Mattson balances family life by embracing the chaos, but with the actor eating five meals per day, you better not touch his bison! Mattson explains that as a model, he simply wasn’t eating enough, but after seeking advice on nutrition, he now tracks his macros, and that means carbs are back in. The star explains that at home, he has his own cupboard for food, meaning that he can stick to his plan in order to stay screen ready.

“We have cabinets in our house, but I have one that us dedicated just for me,” explains Mattson of how he is able to stay focused and avoid the sweet temptations that may be lurking in other areas of the kitchen. The star makes smart swaps, like almonds instead of candy, and eats a large number of blueberries for the effects on muscle recovery. His commitment has certainly paid off, and the actor now weighs in at a lean and muscular 215 pounds as opposed to the 185-pound frame from his modeling days.

Still, when it comes to working out, Mattson often makes it a family affair and shares the fun side of fitness with outdoor jogs and calisthenics, which are great for young bodies.

Not only does he have to stay ripped for the next project, and that could mean just 24-hours’ notice for a shirtless scene, but during the shoot for Agent of Shadows, things got seriously physical. One scene even called for Mattson to mix it up with WWE Hall of Famer Booker T, while filming in the blazing heat of the desert.

“Physically, I was doing all the WWE stunts on the ground,” he explains, noting that his whole body was sore “for days” afterwards.

Mattson went above and beyond with the promotion of this vertical micro-drama too, enrolling at WWE’s Performance Center and stepping inside the ring for real.

“They hit me with a chair, a real chair,” says the actor, reflecting on the surreal nature of his job. “It’s harder than it looks.”

With all of the major streaming platforms now developing, or already offering vertical media, Mattson finds himself as one of the most experienced performers in this area, but as we conclude our conversation, the much sought after star is readying for a flight that will see him working on a regular, horizontal project. Still, in true secret agent style, he can’t tell us anything about it.

“I always stay ready, so I don’t have to get ready,” he signs off.

#8860. ⁠Before You Spend on Gravel Suspension, Try Wider Tubeless Tires for a Simpler, Smoother Ride

Wider tires can add comfort and traction on chunky gravel without the weight of suspension parts.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively new gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

When I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate issues and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

After trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the issue of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

Step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

One easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

If they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore new wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

If you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

On my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8858. Brett Wilkin Shares His Challenging Mass-Building Workout Finishers

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

2024 IFBB Legion Pro winner, and 2025 Mr. Olympia finalist Brett Wilkin is the kind of bodybuilder who leaves it all in the gym. And, in a recent Instagram post, the big man shared the upper and lower body finishers that test his mettle as he looks to pack on even more muscle.

Of course, the aim of any competitive bodybuilder is force their muscle fibers to grow back bigger after being put into a state of hypertrophy from an exhaustive workout, and Wilkin thinks he has found two winning finishers for leveling up his upper and lower body—alternating between supersets and dropsets to approach failure.

Here’s how to try both sequences for yourself.

“Some standing cable flys to failure and straight to the landmine presses,” explained Wilkin to his more than 170,000 Instagram followers. “Stretching it out big to start, then pumping out the inner and upper chest for complete balance. Keeping it simple and effective.”

In the spirit of the superset, Wilkin, who is known to fans as “The Butcher,” takes no rest between the cable fly and landmine press, going big before he goes home. This is a wise combination because the fly hits the shoulders, upper and lower pecs, and even the biceps to some degree, while the landmine two handed chest press has similar coverage but draws upon the triceps more than the biceps.

When it comes to leveraging his lower body, Wilkin opts for drop sets. “Fun fact: Dropsets pair as character builders… and some of y’all out there are lacking character” taunted the man mountain in another recent post.

Setting himself up on the hack squat, Wilkin notes that he rarely observes other gym goers practicing drop sets but explains that they are a go-to for finishing his leg day.

To round out his lower body sessions, the competitive bodybuilder sits low into the hack squat in order to stretch and build his hamstrings and quads. He takes just enough rest time for some plates to be removed before he pounds his pins once again. And, as he works towards failure, Wilkin breathes deeply as he powers through the final moments, readying his legs for even more mass in the future.

“Not just a drop, but tempo work too,” spotted one eagle eyed follower. “Crazy,” wrote another impressed fan. “Big man doing big things!” added yet another.

Ready to build your character in the gym? Be more like Brett Wilkin and try both of these ferocious finishers.
